The original text and the reasoning are kept, so that route C stays open. Route C is the design that P-43 set aside: a nested number tower, under the forest rule of the team's 2012 patent applications (F-46 gives what a return to it would need). Every such change takes the revision form (P-96 gives its parts). The unrevised copy, `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, is never touched. Why: an open disagreement between the text and the implementation would confuse a reader.
102	- P-96 **A change of the specification is shown in layers, as the team showed its own changes in the 1.0 release of 2008 and in the working draft of 2009.** This form is the revision form. A callout that prints in every build marks each changed passage; a `\note` will not do, since a release build hides it. Appendix I's revival section has an entry for each change: its reason, its original text, what a return to route C would mean for it, or that it would be the same under route C (P-95 says what route C is), and the decision that it follows. The front matter has one paragraph on the revision, and a document in the repository holds the full reasoning. Citations call the unrevised copy, `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, the Working Draft of February 2011: the copy is that draft byte for byte, and only its `fortress.1.0.pdf` is the 1.0 release (F-163). The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/specification.md` gives each part in full, including what else an Appendix I entry holds.
103	- P-97 **The specification's examples that break the exclusion rule take the library's shapes, and each original stays, marked "Not allowed".** The Working Draft offered such examples as legal. Each now shows the shape that the library uses for the same thing, with the original beside it under the specification's own mark, "Not allowed". The specification states the rule, which it calls instantiation exclusion, once, in the two parts of Luchangco's Types chapter of 2012 (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`; P-25): `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex` says which instantiations exclude each other, and `basic/traits.tex` says that a declaration may not extend two that do. The covariance example, a trait that extends other instantiations of itself, is rewritten and marked in the same way. Its callout adds one sentence: the type group's later design, in the same Types chapter, declares variance with a `covariant` modifier, which neither walk nor the compiled path implements (row 404 records the gap). The calculi of Appendix A keep their rules as the team wrote them, under a callout that they predate the rule.
104	- P-98 **`TotalComparison` extends `StandardMinMax[\TotalComparison\]`, so that the library's `BIG MIN` and `BIG MAX` work over total comparisons.** It does so in the library's api and component, `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` and `.fss`. It keeps the five members that it restates by hand: `MIN`, `MAX`, `MINMAX`, `<=` and `>=`. Without the parent, walk finds no overload of `BIG MIN` or `BIG MAX` that takes total comparisons (row 461). Why: it is the library's own device, which its other ordered types use. The curator took it on the coordinator's recommendation. It stands and blocks no work.
105	
106	### The suites and the gate
107	
108	- P-102 **Test first, the test kept.** Every edit of source code in the original tree starts from a failing test. The worker adds the test to the test suite, sees it fail, makes the fix, and sees it pass. The test then stays in the suite for good. An edit of the specification or of documentation is not source code and needs no test. The gate's three test runs, `ant testFast`, `ant testSystem` and `ant testSpecData` (P-124), must pass when the work lands; they need not pass after every edit. The test and the fix may land in one commit. Why: the rule replaces one-off validation scripts, which no later build runs. The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/tests-writing.md` says how to write the test.
109	- P-103 **The suite's verdict is the check.** A test's result is pass or fail, as the team designed the suites. A value that matters is checked inside the test, with the checks that the harness already has: an `assert` call in an interpreter test, a `run_out_equals` key in a compiled test's `.test` file. What a test prints beyond its checks does not count. So no expected-output files are added. They are not proposed to the curator again, and neither is a comparison of what a test prints beyond its checks with an earlier run's output. Why: when the suite's designers let a test pass without a further check, what it prints need not be checked.
110	- P-124 **The specification's examples are a step of the gate, and every one must pass.** `ant testSpecData` runs the examples extracted from `Specification/` under walk (F-114 says which 130 it runs), and the gate fails if any of them fails. When an example fails, the implementation is fixed: the example is not respelled to get around a gap in walk, and no list of examples allowed to fail is kept.
111	- P-125 **The suites run Fortress in parallel, pinned at four threads in `build.xml`.** `build.xml` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS` to 4 for the two suites, `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem`, so that every run of them uses four threads, whatever the calling shell sets. A test that parallelism makes fail, on every run or only on some, is written wrong, for example a write that needs `atomic`, or it shows a defect. Either is fixed, never hidden by running at one thread. Why: Fortress is parallel by default, so a suite at one thread has a blind spot, and sparing the four-CPU machine is no reason for one.
112	- P-150 **No resident compiler is built.** A background JVM that serves Fortress commands, as Scala 2's `fsc` did, would save too little of the workers' time to be worth building (F-234), so the speed work goes to the checker itself (P-148). It is not tried again unless something significant changes.
113

<!-- The POSITIONS provenance audit of 2026-10-21 and 22: what it is, where its parts are, and how to run its mining workflow again. -->

# The POSITIONS provenance audit

The audit asks of each POSITIONS entry whether it is the curator's decision, faithfully recorded, or an agent's summary or default that readers took as his word. It ran as a trial on ten entries (`trial/`) and then on the other 75 (`full/`); its corrections are applied at `6b560762f`. Its evidence feeds the clarity workflow (`explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/`).

## The mining workflow

`full/evidence/workflow.js`: per chunk of ten entries, a Sonnet scout per entry (archaeology only), an Opus judgement, an Opus writer on a copy of the record, a cold read and a takeaway check. Its briefs are `full/evidence/briefs/` (the writer's rules 0 to 12); its scripts are `tools/` (`leads.py N` gathers an entry's trail in about 2.5 seconds; `tests.py` checks them; `hischeck.py` checks a report's block of the curator's quotes).

To run it again on entries it has not traced, copy the briefs to a new evidence folder and change the report paths in them, then run the script with that folder and `args: { chunks: [{ name, entries: [numbers] }] }`; at most two agents run at once in one Workflow, so run several side by side. Its results: `full/RESULTS.md`. Today's clarity workflow merges the writer's two passes: the correction by the audit's rules and the rewrite for clarity can be one writer stage when the mining runs again.
<!-- The POSITIONS audit's full run on the 75 entries the trial did not trace, 2026-10-21 to 22: what it proposes, grouped by type for the curator's approval (50 entries change, 25 kept word for word), its 16 questions, its checks and its cost; the reports, judgements, proposals and checks of its eight chunks are in evidence/. Nothing is applied. -->

# The full run's results

Eight chunks of POSITIONS, 75 entries, from 23:37 UTC on 2026-10-21 to 02:25 UTC on 10-22, in four Workflow runs of two chunks each. Each chunk: a Sonnet scout per entry (`evidence/P-N.md`), an Opus judgement (`judgement-cN.md`), an Opus writer on a copy of the record (`corrections-cN.md`, `corrections-cN.apply`, `rewritten-cN.txt`, `review-queue-items-cN.md`), a cold read (`cold-read-cN.md`) and a takeaway check (`takeaway-cN.md`). The briefs are in `evidence/briefs/`, the script in `evidence/workflow.js`. Nothing in POSITIONS, FACTS or their histories has changed.

## What it proposes, by group

The page https://claude.ai/artifact/XSW5Pz56938NcmCPg4GMZb (version 10; group 7 in version 11) shows each entry's change and its whole text before and after.

1. Status and counts moved to the history (8): P-45, P-50, P-51, P-89, P-147, P-149, P-152, P-155.
2. Factual errors corrected (12): P-12, P-19, P-28, P-47, P-53, P-69, P-70, P-72, P-74, P-87, P-91, P-102.
3. One-time approvals and remarks struck (6): P-8, P-9, P-33, P-44, P-78, P-79.
4. Defaults moved to the review queue (8): P-17, P-30, P-40, P-57, P-60, P-75, P-146, P-153.
5. Reworded back to his meaning (10): P-29, P-32, P-39, P-46, P-48, P-54, P-56, P-58, P-62, P-154.
6. Struck (2): P-16, P-123; F-39's pointer to P-123 is rewritten with it.
7. Handles from past conversations struck (19), added at his page comment on P-45 of 2026-10-22 04:53 UTC (`evidence/handles.apply`, applied after the eight): "answer N", "ask N", an "item N" of the questions of 10-09 whose number now names another review-queue item, a probe's "Q1". P-45's at his word, the other 18 the coordinator's proposal. Only P-52 and P-59 are in no other group; with them, 52 entries change and 23 are kept.
- Held for his answers (4): P-27, P-38, P-43, P-90.
- Kept word for word by the writers (25; group 7 would change P-52 and P-59): P-7, P-11, P-25, P-26, P-37, P-41, P-42, P-49, P-52, P-59, P-67, P-68, P-71, P-73, P-76, P-77, P-80, P-84, P-95, P-96, P-97, P-98, P-103, P-124, P-125. Each has source lines for its history that `record.py` cannot write (each chunk's "History lines" section).

Ten review-queue items are drafted for groups 4 and 5; one more (c8, P-124) only if he prefers it to his question. Sixteen questions: fourteen from the writers, on P-26, P-27, P-38, P-42, P-43 (two), P-59, P-77, P-87, P-90, P-95, P-123, P-124 and P-152, and P-85's two from the trial. The takeaway checks found 19 kept sentences that a reader with no context misread; by his rule of 23:21 UTC on 10-21 none is fixed, and each fix is drafted in its chunk's takeaway file.

## The checks

- `tools/hischeck.py` on the 75 reports and 8 judgements: 1,100 quotes of his, all EXACT.
- The eight apply files applied together, in chunk order, on one copy of the record (`scratchpad/positions-audit/full/combined/`), then `record.py check --base 6897e6f48`: 0 failures; POSITIONS from 83 entries to 81; 49 entries rewritten (48 of POSITIONS and F-39), 2 removed.
- The page's groups were checked by script against that copy: the 50 entries the groups name are exactly the 50 that change.

## Points for the next steps

- The writers found history blocks of the consolidation of 2026-10-13 that name the wrong commit (chunks c2, c3, c4 and c6). `record.py` cannot amend a block; the history-only command should cover them.
- "Built." in an entry with nothing left to build: chunks c4, c5, c6 and c8 kept the bare word by rule 0; c7 moved P-89's to the history. The coordinator proposes keeping it in P-89 too.
- Each writer's "The rules, where they fit badly" lists the cases where two rules of the brief pulled apart (mostly rule 0 against rules 2, 6 and 9).

## The cost

19.3M tokens written by the four runs (`tools/spend.py` from epoch 1792625800): 5.38M, 4.75M, 5.19M and 3.97M. The estimate was 16M to 17M. A VM restart at 00:03 UTC killed the runs; they were resumed at 00:05 with their finished agents reused, and the agents killed mid-work ran again from the start.

1	<!-- The evidence map for the top-tier review Pavol asked for on 2026-09-29, of whether his decisions since 2026-09-16 finish or depart from what Fortress's designers intended, written that day by an Opus worker, reading only, for the Fable judge who reads it and then the primary sources it cites. -->
2	
3	# Pavol's decisions since 2026-09-16: the evidence for the review
4	
5	## How to read this
6	
7	- Each entry has five parts: (1) what he decided, his words, what landed; (2) the designers' latest word; (3) the alternatives the record weighed; (4) what the decision set in motion; (5) the doubts on record.
8	- This is a map, not a verdict. Where the record itself reads a decision as finishing or departing, the entry says whose reading it is.
9	- The record is pinned at `be9a75b79` (main, 2026-09-29, 12:30 UTC). FACTS and PLAN are rewritten often; if a line has moved, search for the entry's title.
10	- Abbreviations:
11	  - POSITIONS = `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`; FACTS = `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`; PLAN = `explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md`; ledger = `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`.
12	  - `reviews/` = `explorations/reviews/`; `ladder/` = `explorations/compile-ladder/`; `coordinator/` = `explorations/coordinator/`.
13	  - WD = `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, the unrevised Working Draft of 2011-02-02 (FACTS:143). Spec = `Specification/`, which the revival revises in place. Read WD for the designers' text.
14	  - Types = `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, Luchangco's unfinished 2012 restart (FACTS:145).
15	  - "Walk" is the interpreter; "the checker" is the compiled path's static type checker.
16	
17	### Four facts about the standard itself
18	
19	- The goal names "`Specification/`, the July 2012 draft" (POSITIONS:24; `CLAUDE.md`, Project goal). The team's last edit to that text is 2010-12-09. "July 19, 2012" is a label the revival chose when it built the PDF (`coordinator/spec-lineage.md:12-15`).
20	- The revival has revised Spec in place: 25 revision sections, plus "Passages not yet revised" and "Route C, the alternative not taken" (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:61-1748`). So "judged by `Specification/`" now reads partly the revival's own text.
21	- The WD contradicts itself on the number tower. The types chapter says: "These types are mutually exclusive; no value has more than one of them" (WD `basic/types-vals-vars.tex:501-502`, over ℤ, ℕ, ℚ, ℝ and the fixed widths, `:506-516`; the same words in Types `:979-980`). 14	## 1. Primer: what the designers were aiming for
15	
16	Terms are defined where they first appear. "The team" is the Sun/Oracle Fortress group, 2003-2012. "Walk" is the interpreter; "the checker" is the static type checker, which runs only on the compiled path. "The one library" is the interpreter's library (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss`), which his decision of 2026-09-21 makes the library the compiler checks. "The prelude" is the compiler's own smaller library (`CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin`, `CompilerAlgebra`), to be deleted at "the switch-over", the day the compiled path reads the one library.

18	### The three texts, and which is the designers' latest word
19	
20	- The 2008 release is `Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf`, 262 pages, the team's own artefact (`403afbe0b`, 2008-03-31).
21	- The Working Draft is the LaTeX under `Specification/`. The team's last edit to its text is 2010-12-09 (`44e03b176`). Steele cloned it whole into `Specification-1.0-frozen/` on 2012-01-04, so the frozen directory is byte for byte the draft of 2011-02-02, not the 1.0 text; only the PDF beside it is 1.0 (`coordinator/spec-lineage.md` §§ 1-2, checked). "July 2012" on the revival's PDF is the date of a parentless import commit, chosen by the revival (`414b790e3`), not of any edit.

Its Types chapter (`Prose/Language/types.tick`, 1,056 lines) is fresh 2012 prose and the team's last word on types, exclusion and `comprises`. It has no chapter on static parameters, numbers, coercion beyond a relation, or the library.
23	- The papers: the OOPSLA 2011 type-system paper (`Papers/Types/`), Naden's 2012 journal text on the return-type rule (`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex`, last touched 2012-08-31, the project's last day), the Welterweight calculus (2012), the four patents filed 2012-08-31, and Steele's 2016 retrospective (`research/extracts/SteeleJuliaCon2016-extract.md`).

On the library, static parameters, coercion, overloading resolution and the number chapters it is the Working Draft, whose text on those topics is 2008-2010. On what they actually made run, it is the code: the interpreter's library (2007-2012, never type-checked) and the compiler's prelude and checker (2009-2012).

26	### Numbers and the tower
27	
28	- A **tower** is a chain of number types where each is a subtype of the next: an integer is a rational is a real. In the interpreter's library the team built exactly that in 2008: `ZZ32 <: ZZ64 <: ZZ <: AnyIntegral <: QQ <: RR64 <: Number`, and kept it to the end (`reviews/multiple-instantiation-exclusion.md` § 7, commits `cfe16b43b`, `fca589bbb`). The library chapters of the Working Draft say the same in prose: ℤ "is a subtype of ℚ" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:28-29`) and the listing has `trait ℤ extends { ℚ, ℤ*, ... }` (`:195-196`); ℚ "is a subtype of ℝ" (`basic-lib/numbers.tex:36-37`).
29	- The types chapter of the same draft says the opposite: "Moreover, there are several simple standard numeric types. These types are mutually exclusive; no value has more than one of them." (`basic/types-vals-vars.tex:500-502`, the list that follows names ℤ, ℕ, ℚ, ℝ, ℂ and every fixed width). That sentence is not in the text of the 2008 release (searched) and is in the draft by February 2011; the cut history does not date it more closely. The 2012 Types chapter keeps it word for word (`types.tick:977-980`). So the draft contradicts itself, and the later text sides with exclusion.
30	- The compiler side went flat in 2009, after a tower that stood from March to August. Chase, 2009-08-31: "ZZ32 is NOT a subtype of ZZ64, RR32 is NOT a subtype of RR64; this would be a good time to get coercion working" (`6896886fb`). Maessen, 2009-11-17: "expect more coercions to come on line as we gradually migrate to a flat numeric hierarchy" (`128f313b5`). Steele added the prelude's `Comparison` traits with their `extends` clauses commented out on 2011-07-15 (`b3c2e1342`) and added the operators of the sibling `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` on 2011-07-22 (`da5291587`). Steele's 2016 slide draws `Number → {Integral → ZZ32, ZZ64, ZZ; Float → RR32, RR64}` (`SteeleJuliaCon2016-extract.md:159-161`).
31	- Rounding: the draft's rational chapter declares `floor`, `⌊⌋`, `ceiling`, `⌈⌉`, `round`, `truncate` all returning ℤ, and says `round` sends an exact half to the even integer (`basic-lib/numbers.tex:457-472`). It has no chapter for the floating-point types. The 2008 release, in its library listing, declares for floats what C and IEEE do: `floor(a: Number): RR64`, `⌊a⌋: ZZ64`, `ceiling(a: Number): RR64`, `⌈a⌉: ZZ64`, `truncate(a: Number): ZZ64` (the 1.0 PDF, pdftotext lines 8295-8299). The interpreter's api declares the same on `RR64`: `floor(self): RR64`, `|\self/| : ZZ64`, `ceiling(self): RR64`, `|/self\| : ZZ64`, `truncate(self): ZZ64` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:368-372`); its component body is inconsistent with the api (`|\self/| : ZZ`, `truncate(self): RR64`, `round(self): ZZ`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:470-475`). The team's prelude declared none of them for `RR64` and left `floor(self): RR64` and `ceiling(self): RR64` in a comment (`git show 5a68404fd:ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi`, lines 438-439).
32	- Overflow: "For integer results, overflow throws an `IntegerOverflow`" (`basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:154-155`, `:195-196`), kept by Steele in the 2012 restart; wrapping has its own operators ∔ ∸ ⨰ and saturation ⊞ ⊟ ⊡ (`:172-176`, `:205-209`). The interpreter wrapped silently; Maessen's 2007 comment calls the range checks not yet done.
33	- Where they left it open: how to have both the exclusion rule (below) and ℤ inside ℚ. Naden, 2012: the numeric hierarchy is written with the self-type idiom, it has "crossed instantiations of the kind that we determined must be outlawed", the self-type bound fixes one failure and not the other, "Victor and John have started working on this sort of theory with their trolls", and "more work needs to be done in order to understand how to best support the numerical hierarchy in the Fortress type system" (`justificationOfRTR.tex:568-632`). Nobody solved it.

35	### Generics and their specialisation
36	
37	- A **static parameter** is a parameter of a declaration filled at compile time or at run time: a type (`List[\T\]`), a number (`Vector[\T, nat n\]`), a boolean, an operator, a dimension. An **instantiation** fills it (`List[\ZZ\]`). Fortress **reifies** generics: a value carries its instantiation at run time, so dispatch can tell `List[\Boolean\]` from `List[\String\]` (Steele 2016, slide 41). Java erases them; this is where Fortress departed from Java.
38	- **Specialisation** is a generic declaration beside a special version for one instantiation: `tail[\X\](x: List[\X\])` beside `tail(x: List[\ZZ\])`, chosen at run time by the value. Naden's 2011 workshop paper says the library's authors "found it useful ... to define both monomorphic and polymorphic versions of functions" (`reviews/mie-probes/literature.md` § 1). The team's tests and the checker's dispatcher are built for it.
39	- To make that sound they adopted **multiple instantiation exclusion**: no type may be a subtype of two different instantiations of one generic ("a rule that forbids multiple instantiation inheritance, in which a type (other than Bottom) is a subtype of distinct applications of a type constructor", `Papers/Types/exclusion.tick:141-152`; in the checker since 2010-05-28 and as `checkP` since 2010-07-26). The 2012 Types chapter renames it "instantiation exclusion" and adds a `covariant` modifier (`types.tick:322-339`, `:353-372`). Naden: "Fortress implements blanket multiple instantiation exclusion for the semantic benefits and the simplicity of the restriction" (`justificationOfRTR.tex:496-497`). The tower breaks it because each level says "I am `Equality` at my own type", so one `ZZ32` is `Equality` at five instantiations.
40	- **Run-time instantiation**: when dispatch picks a generic declaration the static call did not select, its parameters must be inferred at run time; the 2011 paper says so and leaves how "beyond the scope of this paper" (`Papers/Types/rules.tick:118-129`). Welterweight aims for "the most specific instantiation of an applicable entrypoint" (`Papers/Welterweight/dispatch.tick:67`). Steele's 2016 slide 44, "Where We Got Stuck": generic methods with symmetric dispatch need the parametric meet rule and the return-type rule, which need "nontrivial run-time constraint solving" ("a euphemism for exponential cost"); "So we had a grand vision, but could not quite pull it off." Naden's last memo (`Papers/RuntimeInstantiation/`) restricts the instance by the static return type; implemented on neither path.
41	- **`where` clauses**, a second way to bind a type variable ("Trait declarations are allowed to extend other instantiations of themselves", `basic/trait-parameters.tex:339-352`, and `object Empty extends List[\T\] where {T extends Object}`, `:384-397`): "Widening and where clauses are not yet supported" (`basic/conversions-coercions.tex:15`); code generation refuses any declaration with one (FACTS:158).
42	
43	### Overloading and dispatch
44	
45	- Fortress has **symmetric multimethods**: an overloaded call is resolved on all its arguments, once statically (the most specific declaration applicable to the static types) and again at run time (the most specific applicable to the run-time types, `basic/overloading.tex:262-276`). The **return-type rule** ties the two: a more specific declaration's result must fit the less specific one's, so the run-time choice never returns something the static choice did not promise.
46	- On static parameters the 2008 release had a first model that "may be replaced when the static type checker and the type inference engine are implemented" (the 1.0 PDF, lines 5234-5241). The 2009 draft replaced it with a ban: "it is an error for their static parameters to differ ... Hence, static parameters do not enter into the determination of which declarations are applicable" (`basic/overloading.tex:100-107`), and in the same draft listed "Relaxing restrictions on static parameters of overloaded functionals" as future work with Jan Maessen's `array1` pair (`appendices/future.tex:236-266`). The 2011 paper allows differing static parameters under three rules (No Duplicates, Meet, Return Type), the checker enforces them, walk never enforced the ban, and the 2012 restart drops the sentence.
47	
48	### Coercion
49	
50	- A **coercion** is a conversion a trait declares from another type (`trait ZZ64 ... coerce(z: ZZ32)`), inserted by the compiler where no declaration applies without it. It is not chained (`conversions-coercions.tex:127-130`). "For a given functional call, we first determine whether there exists a declaration that is applicable without coercion. If so, the most specific declaration is selected; if not, then coercions are explicitly added" (`:454-462`). It is resolved on static types: "Notice that coercion is resolved statically", with an example where `c: C = D` and `f(c)` calls `f(A)` by coercion "despite the fact that the declaration f(B) is applicable to the dynamic call f(D)" (`:598-635`). The draft's own example of widths declares `ZZ64 coerce(z: ZZ32)` and `ZZ128` from both (`:549-565`); no sentence makes `ZZ32` a subtype of `ZZ64`. "Fortress supports the automatic conversion of integer values to floating-point values" (`:64-66`), a general sentence.
51	- Numerals: "numerals have their own types ... This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations" (`basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-148`); the types named (`NaturalNumeral[\n,10,v\]`) carry the value and were never implemented; a note says "We need to describe the Numeral type hierarchy" (`:83-95`). The prelude has one `IntLiteral`, a sibling each number type coerces from (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:390-429`; Maessen 2009: "ZZ32 now coerces IntLiteral as described in the spec"). The interpreter's is `object IntLiteral extends { ZZ32 }` with its arithmetic commented out: "Do not enable these until coercion is implemented; doing so will cause all our arithmetic to occur on IntLiterals." (`FortressBuiltin.fss:497-498`).
52	- The prelude's coercions are every exact integer pair and none from an integer into a float (`reviews/flattening-questions-ways.md` § 5, checked at `CompilerBuiltin.fsi:103-108`, `:147-149`, `:433-435`).
53	
54	### Sizes
55	
56	- A **`nat` parameter** is a static parameter that is a number: `Vector[\T, nat n\]`. "These parameters are instantiated at runtime with numeric values. A nat parameter may be used ... to appear in any context that a variable of type ℕ32 can appear" (`basic/trait-parameters.tex:78-90`). The library's arrays and matrices carry their sizes this way and their products require the inner sizes to agree (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1680-1684`). The team's checker never checked them ("Todo: Handle int, nat, bool args"), the code generator reserved a slot for them (`CodeGen.java:5317-5328`), and the library's `NatReflect.fss:38-40` says of making a size from a run-time number "Really this just proves that it can be done without extending the language. Having proven that, we ought to build it in".
57	- Unboxing (storing a float as a machine double, not as an object) was intended and never built: `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java:12-19` and the loader's empty "expando" stub (`InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172`).
58	
59	### `comprises` and exclusion
60	
61	- **`excludes`** declares that two traits share no value; an object type excludes every type not above it (`basic/types-vals-vars.tex:212-224`). Exclusion is what lets the checker prove two overloads never both apply.
62	- **`comprises`** closes a trait: `trait Number comprises { RR64, QQ, AnyIntegral }` lists the types below it. The draft reads the list at the level of types: the listed traits "are exactly the traits that immediately extend T" (`basic/traits.tex:231-234`, a draft note). The 2012 texts read it at the level of values: an instantiation "is covered by the union of the types in this set" (`types.tick:384-389`); "no value can belong to the trait unless it also belongs to one of the comprised types" (`Papers/Welterweight/grammar.tick:21-22`). The draft's future-work list says "We agreed to revise the Meet rule to address this with the coverage check" (`appendices/future.tex:285`).
63	- The **self-type idiom**: `trait Ring[\X\] comprises X`, so `Ring[\ℚ\]` "is really just ℚ itself" (Naden, `:576-582`); the patents of 2012-08-31 make it a named exception to the exclusion rule ("Self-types meet"), never built.
64	
65	### The libraries
66	
67	- The specification knows one library, "chiefly `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/library/structure.tex:15-18`). The compiler prelude was cut on 2008-12-19 as a "Hopefully temporary hack as we work on importing java objects cleanly" (`WellKnownNames.java:110-111`) and grown for three and a half years; the team called what went into it "bogus" (2009).
68	- The library's own flavour: algebra traits (`AdditiveGroup[\T\]`, `MultiplicativeRing[\T\]`, `StandardTotalOrder[\T\]`), each self-typed, carried by every number type; reductions licensed by associativity and identity; open marker traits (`AnyMaybe`, `AnyList`) with a "not yet" comment where a `where`-clause `comprises` was wanted (`FortressLibrary.fsi:434`). The specified algebraic-constraints library (monoids, groups, rings, fields, `HasIdentity`) exists only commented out (`Library/incomplete/`). Steele's 2016 slide 12 promised "Rational, complex, and quaternion"; only rational shipped.
69

72	- Both the exclusion rule and the nested tower (Naden's "more work needs to be done").
73	- Run-time instantiation of a dispatched generic (the 2011 paper's "beyond the scope"; Naden's unfinished memo).
74	- Inference of static arguments at a call (`basic/inference.tex` is a 27-line stub).
75	- A numeral's type hierarchy ("We need to describe").
76	- The float types' rounding methods (no chapter; three inconsistent spellings in their own library).
77	- Whether `comprises` is read on types or on values (two readings, the later one on values).
78	- `where` clauses and widening (never supported).
79	- Sizes in the checker and at run time (a "Todo", a reserved slot, "we ought to build it in").
80	- Which integer width a range has (no sentence; the prelude says `ZZ32`).

12	## 0. What the record knew, and what the paper says
13	
14	The record's account (`literature.md` § 1) was right as far as it went: the paper keeps the invariant-instantiation exclusion through its ancestor rule, moves the return-type check to run time, and has no self types and no numeric tower. What it did not have, each checked in the text:
15	
16	- The instance rule. "The Fortress team had assumed, because it seemed from several working examples to be in accord with intuition, that once the tightest possible upper and lower bounds for a method type parameter have been found, then the union (or pseudo-union) of the lower bounds should be chosen as the type to be used for that type parameter. We considered this and the hybrid technique ... but we were unable to complete the proofs of correctness of both the techniques. Since the minimum requirement for a type to instantiate a method type parameter is that it satisfies all the lower and upper bounds of the type parameter, the dynamic dispatch algorithm presented here always chooses the intersection of the upper bounds." (§ 5.4, p. 11:25, lines 1274-1284.) The rule itself is [Solve-Step] (§ 5.2.3, p. 11:19, lines 965-1016): the substitution for a parameter is the intersection of its computed upper bound and its declared upper bounds, checked against the lower bounds; "Because g' is a ground type, the solving step never instantiates method type parameters with Bottom."
17	- The static return type at run time. Dispatch "seeks the most specific method declaration with a dispatchable instance that is applicable to the ilk of the arguments and whose return type is a subtype of the annotated static return type" ([R-Method], § 5.2.1, p. 11:17, lines 888-896); "the language semantics needs to make the static types of method invocations available at run time" (§ 2.3, p. 11:7, lines 329-331). The upper bound of a return-only parameter comes from that static return type ([Dispatch], line 875: `g match ρ - bounds`).
18	- The default bound. "By default, each type parameter has an upper bound Any and a lower bound Bottom" (§ 3.2, p. 11:9, lines 418-419). `Bottom` "is intentionally not expressible in the surface syntax" (line 438).
19	- The overloading rules in checkable form (§ 4, Figure 5, p. 11:13, lines 630-661): No Duplicates as non-subtyping of domains either way; Meet as exclusion, subtyping or a third declaration whose domain is equivalent to the intersection ([Meet-Third], line 645); Return Type as one universal subtyping check, `arrow(d1) ⊑ ∀[κ,κ']((α ⊓ α') → ρ')` ([Return-Test], lines 656-660). Specificity is subtyping of existentially quantified domains, "a sound approximation of the subset relation of applicable sets, [but] not complete" (§ 4.2, p. 11:13, lines 673-675), narrowed by "existential reduction", which collects the constraints that keep a domain off `Bottom` and solves them (lines 733-743, Figure 6).
20	- A restriction the proof needs. A method's type parameter bindings are well formed only if "no reference to a method type parameter appears in any of the upper bounds" and every reference falls within a left-to-right scope; "restriction (1) makes dynamic dispatch more efficient and restriction (2) makes it consistent" (§ 3.3, p. 11:11, lines 565-570); the one-pass right-to-left solve depends on it (lines 1010-1016, 1258-1262). Trait type parameters carry no such restriction.
21	- What the calculus leaves out. "FGFV omits functional methods [Allen et al. 2007] and declarations of closed types [Allen et al. 2011], but these could be added back to FGFV in an obvious way" (§ 1, p. 11:3, lines 142-144); "FGFV does not support features like modularity, nominal exclusion, and closed types in their work, [but] they can be added in an obvious way" (§ 6, p. 11:25, lines 1302-1303). No coercion, no `nat` parameters, no numbers.
22	- The exclusion rule's form and date. [Anc-Same-Trait] (Figure 4, p. 11:11, lines 530-532): a class extending two instances of a trait must extend an instance below both; "the 'Ancestor Meet Rule' ... was introduced into Fortress in 2012 by Guy Steele and David Chase" (§ 5.4, p. 11:24, lines 1230-1232). For an invariant parameter only the same instance is below both; for a covariant one the lower instance is.
23	- Variance in full: marks `+ - =` on trait parameters, objects always invariant (§ 3.2, lines 406-409); a covariant parameter only in covariant positions, a contravariant one only in contravariant ones ([D-Method], § 3.3, pp. 11:11-12, lines 571-595); dispatch with variance marks (§ 5.2.2); exponential blowup only where union types meet contravariance, accepted (§ 5.4, lines 1239-1257); the two alternatives the team weighed in 2012, dropping contravariance or dropping union types.
24	- Cost. "In simple invariant cases, we expect the run-time cost to be relatively low but nonzero"; for variant cases "caching or dynamic recompilation" (§ 5.4, pp. 11:24-25, lines 1263-1273).

- P-75 **`NN32` coerces into `RR64` implicitly, since every `NN32` value converts to `RR64` exactly.** Why: a conversion that fits is implicit, the rule of P-74 on mixed widths. With the coercion, an operator that both `RR64` and `ZZ64` declare is ambiguous on both paths for a `ZZ32` with an `NN32`, since neither `ZZ64` nor `RR64` coerces into the other. Without it, P-74's rule, the narrowest type into which both arguments coerce, gives `ZZ64` (row 575 holds the conflict and its measurement). Each way to build it changes a decided behaviour.

### P-78

2026-10-22 22:14Z · rewritten · from `explorations/coordinator/consolidation-2026-10-22/evidence/positions-followup/proposals.md`, "P-78" · by the POSITIONS follow-up writer (Opus): the cold read found the rule against the skill's every clause form; his answer 7, a clause form whose element type nothing at the call fixes writes its static argument, restored; row 731's refusal said as the checker's gap, and writing the argument in every clause form as row 731's workaround; applied at the curator's word of 22:12 UTC on 2026-10-22, \"apply all the improvements drafted\", without his review of each change

- P-78 **`SUM` and `PROD` are one generic reduction each over the library's algebra, in place of the team's catch-all over `Number`, and take their identity from the static argument.** `SUM` is generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `PROD` over `MultiplicativeRing`. A reduction written with generators writes its static argument where its generators and body do not fix the element type, as in `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. A declared type that receives the value does not fix it: the compiled checker refuses the call without the static argument even then (row 731). A sum without generators is written as before, with no static argument: `SUM e` over a collection `e`, and the dot product `x DOT y`. `BIG MAXN`, `BIG MINN` and `BIG MINMAXN`, the team's `Number`-typed big operators for the maximum, the minimum and both, each with an identity, are gone; no program called them. `MAX` and `MIN` get no identity on the integers or the floats, so an empty `BIG MAX` or `BIG MIN` raises `EmptyReduction` (F-60: a maximum's identity is its type's least value, which a coercion into a wider type does not carry). Under walk, an empty `SUM` or `PROD` over another algebra, such as a user `AdditiveGroup`, still fails (row 436) until the specification's `HasIdentity` is built.

### P-79

2026-10-22 22:14Z · rewritten · from `explorations/coordinator/consolidation-2026-10-22/evidence/positions-followup/proposals.md`, "P-79" · by the POSITIONS follow-up writer (Opus): the cold read found that nothing runs the demos and batch undefined; no suite or gate step runs them (build.xml, the worker skill), and batch defined in the words of P-30 and P-39; applied at the curator's word of 22:12 UTC on 2026-10-22, \"apply all the improvements drafted\", without his review of each change

- P-79 **Every team demo is kept running as the tree changes.** The team demos are the programs in `ProjectFortress/demos/`. If a change breaks a demo and the way to repair the demo is known, the same batch rewrites the demo. ===  2026-10-23T06:25:58.712Z
**Question 1 of 2: How should the library's two subscripts be fixed, so that they pass the overload check once the checker reads symbolic operators?**

**Context:**
- **The pair.** Every collection in the library is an `Indexed[\E, I\]`, with elements of type `E` and indices of type `I`. It declares two subscripts (`FortressLibrary.fsi:1297` and `:1309`):
  ```
  opr[i: I]: E                         a[3]     one element
  opr[r: Range[\I\]]: Indexed[\E, I\]  a[2:4]   a slice
  ```
- **Why the checker refuses the pair.** Fortress wants overloads to be unambiguous for every possible instance, not only at a call, as Swift checks them. Here `I` has no bound, so `I` could itself be a range type. Then `a[r]` fits both declarations, with different results.
  - At `I = ZZ32` the pair is fine, because a range is never a number.
  - In the 124 generic declarations (the mapped and reversed views, and arrays over any index type), it's refused.
  - Today the checker skips symbolic operators, so these errors don't show.
- **What the team wrote.** Its "future" appendix calls this pair "not really a valid overloading" and names the fix: bound `I` by a type `Index` that excludes ranges. It stopped on one problem. `a[1, 2]` passes the tuple `(1, 2)`, so a tuple of indices would need "a magic" to count as an `Index` (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:186-207`).
- **Peers, as context only.** Swift's `Collection` declares the same pair, `subscript(Index)` and `subscript(Range<Index>)`, and resolves the overload at each call. Julia tells a range from an integer by type at dispatch.
- **The switch-over needs this answer.** You decided the symbolic operators are checked before the switch-over, and this pair is 124 of the 186 errors.

**Options:**
1. **The team's fix, with the "magic" as a subtyping rule.**
   - The library: a new trait `Index`, which `ZZ32` extends and ranges exclude, and every index parameter becomes `I extends Index`.
   - One new rule: a tuple of indices is an index, so `(ZZ32, ZZ32)` can index a matrix.
   - Measured: the 124 errors go and none comes. Walk's suite passes 668 of 668 and the specification's examples 130 of 130. microGPT's check passes 7 of 7, and 30 array demos are unchanged.
   - Cost: one rung that touches the library (40 edits), the checker, walk and the specification's types chapter. A program with its own index type must declare it an `Index`, but no program in the suites has one. `BoundedRange` loses its `atMost` narrowing.
2. **The checker checks the pair only at the types that fix `I`.**
   - A checker change, with no library or language edit.
   - It clears the 124 by reading; it wasn't measured.
   - It refuses a user's `Indexed[\E, Any\]`.
3. **Range subscripts only where the index type is fixed,** as `Array1` to `Array3` and `String` already have them.
   - Library edits only; not measured.
   - The generic mapped, reversed and index-pair views lose slicing.
4. **Slices get another bracket pair, or a method.**
   - Every program that slices changes. That includes microGPT, which slices strings in its data code.

**How they compare:**
- Option 1 is the only one that keeps both subscripts on every generic collection, and it follows the team's own text. It adds a new rule on both paths, the one the team said it needed.
- Option 2 is the cheapest. But it breaks your rule that a generic declaration is checked over all its instances, and it refuses a legal program.
- Option 3 needs no new rule, but takes slicing away from the team's generic views.
- Option 4 changes microGPT's lines.

**Recommendation:** option 1.

The probe that measured these options: https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/perf-probes/symbolic-operators-2/REPORT.md

===  2026-10-23T06:38:50.925Z
None of your decisions forbids S5. The probe set it aside without measuring it, by reading your decision on `where` clauses too narrowly.

**What that decision says.** We build only the `where` forms the team wrote down: conditional extension, a function's or method's condition, and the list's `comprises` clause. Your reason allows more. You'd have a new form built where the team left enough design intent, or where it's on the critical path to compiled speed. The probe read the three forms as a closed list and stopped there.

**Where S5 comes from.** The team never proposed it for subscripts.
- Their note on the subscript pair asks for a bound: `I` extends an `Index` type.
- The line the probe cites is the next item in the same appendix of open questions, "Type variables in excludes clauses". It's a commented example, `excludes Indexed[\U\] where [\U\]{I excludes U}`, with no grammar or meaning given.
- Fortress has no `excludes` constraint. The grammar, the syntax tree and the specification allow only `extends`, type aliases, `coerces`/`widens`, `=`, and the size and boolean constraints.

**What S5 would be:** `trait Indexed[\E, I\] ... where { I excludes Range[\I\] }`.
- **Its real advantage:** no tuple rule. A tuple already excludes every trait type, ranges included, so `a[1, 2]` needs no "magic". A user's own index object also excludes ranges without declaring anything.
- **Its costs, by reading only:**
  - A new language form: the grammar, the syntax tree's definitions, the specification's section on `where` clauses, and Appendix I.
  - The checker would check the constraint wherever `Indexed[\E, I\]` is used, as it already checks `extends` constraints, and its overload check would have to read it.
  - Walk would only need to parse it, since walk doesn't check a trait instance's constraints today.
  - The library would carry the same constraint on the roughly 20 generic types that option 1 bounds.
  - **Code generation:** today it refuses every trait or object with a `where` clause in its own header. With S5, `Indexed` and every collection type would carry one, so after the switch-over the compiled path couldn't compile any collection until that refusal is fixed. Option 1's bound doesn't hit this.

**Read whole, your decision points to option 1.** For the `Index` bound, the team wrote its intent down for exactly this pair. For an `excludes` constraint, it left only an open question. S5 is on the critical path, but so is option 1, so the path doesn't need it.

I'd keep option 1 as the default. If you want S5 weighed on numbers, a probe can build it in a shadow copy at the reset (10:00 UTC, 12:00 your time), beside the planner: the checker and library halves, plus a code-generation check on one trait. My guess is 0.5M to 1M tokens. Either way, the subscripts rung waits for your answer.

===  2026-10-23T06:49:00.941Z
The "magic" doesn't turn a tuple into a range. It's a typing rule that lets the type system call a tuple of indices an index, so that option 1 can declare that an index is never a range. The steps below build up to it.

**1. Fortress's brackets**
- `f(x)` is a call.
- `a[i]` is the subscript operator: a method call on `a`, named `opr[]`, with the index as its argument. It's not a list. `m[1, 2]` calls `m`'s subscript with the two indices 1 and 2.
- `[\ \]`, the white square brackets, hold static parameters, Fortress's generics. `Indexed[\Char, ZZ32\]` is like Swift's `Indexed<Character, Int32>`.
- `<|1, 2|>` is a list literal. `[1 2 3]` is an array literal, with its elements separated by spaces.

**2. How `m[1, 2]` reaches the subscript**
- A Fortress function or method takes one argument, and several arguments travel as one tuple. The specification says an argument "need not be parenthesized unless it is a tuple" (`function-calls.tex:29-30`). So `m[1, 2]` passes the tuple `(1, 2)`. No desugaring builds it: every call with several arguments works this way.
- A matrix, `Array2`, is declared as a collection whose index type is the tuple type `(ZZ32, ZZ32)` (`FortressLibrary.fsi:1695-1697`). At that type, `opr[i: I]` reads `opr[i: (ZZ32, ZZ32)]`, and `i` holds `(1, 2)`.

**3. The pair, at its instances**
```
trait Indexed[\E, I\] extends Generator[\E\]
  opr[i: I]: E                         (one element)
  opr[r: Range[\I\]]: Indexed[\E, I\]  (a slice)
end
```
- A string is an `Indexed[\Char, ZZ32\]`: `s[3]` is a `Char`, and `s[2:4]` is a slice.
- A matrix is an `Indexed[\RR64, (ZZ32, ZZ32)\]`: `m[1, 2]` is an `RR64`, and `m[(0,0):(1,1)]` is a block of it.

**4. Why the checker refuses the pair**
- Swift checks an overloaded call where it's written. Fortress checks the pair once, at its declaration, for every type that `I` could take (your decision on overloading). The reason is that dispatch runs at run time, on the value:
  - The checker types each call by the declaration it sees from the static types.
  - The run time then runs the most specific declaration for the actual value.
  - If the two choices differ and their results differ, the static type is wrong.
- `I` has no bound, so `I = Any` is allowed: an `Indexed[\String, Any\]` takes anything as an index. The library's whole range `(:)`, as in `a[:]`, is a range of `Any`. Take a generic function:
  ```
  pick[\E, I\](a: Indexed[\E, I\], i: I): E = a[i]
  ```
- The checker sees `i: I`, picks `opr[i: I]`, and types `a[i]` as an `E`.
- Now call `pick(x, (:))`, with `x: Indexed[\String, Any\]`. `(:)` is a valid `I`, since it's an `Any`. But at run time it's also a range, so dispatch runs a slice subscript, and `pick` returns a slice where its type promised a `String`. You guessed this: the static type says "element", and the value is a collection.
- The return-type rule catches it: where one declaration is more specific than the other, its result must fit the other's result. A slice is no `E`, so the checker refuses the pair in every generic type that declares it. That's the 124 errors.
- Where `I` is fixed at a type that can't be a range, such as `ZZ32` or a tuple type, no such value exists, and the pair already passes.

**5. The fix: say that an index is never a range**

The team's note says to bound `I` by an `Index` type that excludes ranges. Option 1 does exactly that:
```
trait Index end
trait ZZ32 extends { ..., Index }
Range ... excludes { Number, String, Index }
trait Indexed[\E, I extends Index\] ...
```
- Every legal `I` is now an `Index`, and no `Index` value is a range, so no value fits both declarations and the pair is valid.
- `Indexed[\String, Any\]` is refused where it's declared, so the hole in step 4 closes.

**6. The "magic"**
- A matrix's index type is the tuple type `(ZZ32, ZZ32)`. The bound needs `(ZZ32, ZZ32)` to be an `Index`, but a tuple type can't extend anything: only traits and objects have `extends` clauses.
- So with the bound alone, every matrix is refused. The probe measured 73 new errors, all at `(ZZ32, ZZ32)` and `(ZZ32, ZZ32, ZZ32)`, and walk stops microGPT at `0.0 MAX m0`.
- That's the team's "we need a magic to convert that tuple to an Index". It has two readings:
  - Convert each index tuple into an index object at every call. Every `m[i, j]` and every `for (i, j) <- m.indices` would then change its values.
  - A typing rule: a tuple whose elements are all indices is itself an index. No value changes, and `(1, 2)` stays a tuple. Only the type system learns that `(ZZ32, ZZ32)` is an `Index`.
- The probe took the second reading.
- About "a tuple already excludes every trait type": that's why fixed matrices pass today, since a tuple can never be a range. The trouble is that a tuple can't be named an `Index`, so the bound would lock matrices out. The rule makes a tuple of indices an `Index` and keeps it apart from ranges.

**7. The patches**
- **Library**, `subscripts-index-bound.patch`: about 54 lines added and 52 removed in `FortressLibrary.fsi` and `.fss`. It adds the `Index` trait, makes `ZZ32` extend it and ranges exclude it, and puts `I extends Index` on about 20 generic types. It also drops `BoundedRange`'s `atMost`, which can't take the bound.
- **Checker**, `checker-tupleindex.patch`: 4 lines in the subtype test (`TypeAnalyzer.scala`): a tuple is an `Index` when each of its elements is. Still to write: the exclusion side. The probe left that out, so its checker says a tuple is an `Index` and also excludes it, a contradiction the rung must fix.
- **Walk**, `walk-tupleindex.patch`: 9 lines in `FTypeTuple.java`, the same rule in walk's three tests:
  - the subtype test;
  - the meet, the common subtype that walk computes when it bounds a type parameter;
  - the exclusion test.
- Both probe patches find `Index` by its text name. The rung would refer to the library's trait properly.
- The rung also adds the rule to the specification's types chapter and Appendix I, with tests first on both paths.

So option 1 adds no new syntax. It's one typing rule, about 13 lines of Scala and Java plus the exclusion side, and the library's bound. It's the team's own fix for this exact pair, and the probe saw nothing move: the suites pass, microGPT's check passes, and 30 array demos are unchanged.

===  2026-10-23T06:50:54.819Z
**Question 2 of 2: Should vectors and matrices stay additive groups now that the checker reads `+` and `-`?**

**Context:**
- **An additive group** is a type with `+`, `-` and a `zero`, such as `RR64`. The library's trait `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` declares those three (`FortressLibrary.fsi:265-270`), and generic code takes any such `T`. For example, `SUM` over vectors adds them up, starting from the zero vector. `Vector` and `Matrix` extend `AdditiveGroup`, and they also declare their own `+` and `-`.
- **The pair.** Two declarations of `+` meet at a vector:
  ```
  AdditiveGroup:  opr +(self, other: T): T                   v + w     two vectors
  scalar block:   opr +[\T extends {Number, AdditiveGroup[\T\]}, I\]

  ```

The revival made the block generic in September, and microGPT relies on it: `z - (BIG MAX z)`. So the conflict is new. The team never had both.

**Options:**

   - Generic code over additive groups no longer takes a vector: `SUM` over vectors, and `zero`. Nothing measured uses those, microGPT included.

- Option 2 keeps everything. But it changes the checker on a point of soundness, and no way to do it has been measured.

===  2026-10-23T06:59:01.452Z
`atMost` itself doesn't go. Only one line goes: the declaration that promised `BoundedRange`'s `atMost` returns a full range.

**What changes:**

34	## 1. What the paper is
35	
36	The abstract claims "the first formal specification of a strongly typed
37	object-oriented language with symmetric multiple dispatch, multiple
38	inheritance, and parametric polymorphism with variance", with a static and a
39	dynamic semantics and a type soundness proof "demonstrating that our novel
40	dynamic dispatch algorithm is consistent with the static semantics"
41	(p. 11:1). The calculus is **FGFV**, "Featherweight Generic Fortress with
42	Variance" (p. 11:3). It formalises the overloading rules of the 2011 OOPSLA
43	paper (Allen et al., in the tree as `Papers/Types/`), which were stated
44	informally and without a language semantics. It adds declaration-site
45	variance and a dispatch algorithm, and proves that the static rules and the
46	run-time choice agree (§6, p. 11:25).

48	The language (Fig. 2, p. 11:8; §3.2, pp. 11:8-9):
49	- **Traits and objects.** Traits are "like Java interfaces that do not have
50	  any fields", and objects are "like Java final classes that cannot be
51	  extended".
52	- **Type parameters.** Trait type parameters carry a variance mark (`+`, `-`,
53	  `=`) and upper bounds. Object type parameters are always invariant. Method
54	  type parameters have lower and upper bounds, and the defaults are `Any` and
55	  `Bottom`.
56	- **Expressions.** Variables, first-class functions, object creation with
57	  written type arguments, and method calls `e.m(e)` with no written type
58	  arguments.
59	- **Types.** `Bottom` "is intentionally not expressible in the surface
60	  syntax" (p. 11:9). Union and intersection types exist only as internal
61	  types (p. 11:9). Tuples are not values.
62	- **What is left out.** "FGFV omits functional methods … and declarations
63	  of closed types …, but these could be added back to FGFV in an obvious
64	  way" (p. 11:3). Related work adds "modularity, nominal exclusion, and
65	  closed types" to that list (p. 11:25). There are no top-level functions:
66	  what is overloaded is methods.

68	## 2. The rule excluding multiple instantiations
69	
70	- **The rule.** Every pair of a class's proper ancestors must satisfy
71	  [Anc-Diff-Trait] (instances of two different traits: no condition) or
72	  [Anc-Same-Trait] (Fig. 4, p. 11:11). [D-Trait] and [D-Object] both check it
73	  (Fig. 3, p. 11:10). [Anc-Same-Trait] requires that "if a class C extends two
74	  instances of a trait T, T⟦α⟧ and T⟦ρ⟧, then C also extends some T⟦γ⟧
75	  (which may be T⟦α⟧, T⟦ρ⟧, or a third instance) that extends both"
76	  (p. 11:11).
77	- **Per variance (our derivation from the rule's two subtype premises).** An
78	  invariant parameter forces γ = α = ρ, so two different instances cannot
79	  both be ancestors: that is the blanket rule. A covariant parameter needs an
80	  ancestor instance whose argument is below both arguments, and a
81	  contravariant one needs one whose argument is above both.
82	- **Why.** "Because the rules guarantee that there always exists a single
83	  minimal ancestor when a class extends multiple instances of a trait, no
84	  ambiguous method calls are possible due to multiple instances of a trait"
85	  (p. 11:11).
86	- **Credited.** The discussion calls it "the 'Ancestor Meet Rule' …
87	  introduced into Fortress in 2012 by Guy Steele and David Chase … to design
88	  an expressive type system with union and intersection types". It gives the
89	  laws T⟦α ⊓ α′⟧ ≡ T⟦α⟧ ⊓ T⟦α′⟧ for a covariant T and T⟦α ⊔ α′⟧ ≡ T⟦α⟧ ⊓
90	  T⟦α′⟧ for a contravariant one, and not "the 'obvious other two cases'"
91	  (p. 11:24). The citation is "Personal communication".
92	- **Used by the overloading check.** To close part of the gap between
93	  subtyping of domains and inclusion of applicable sets, the checker reduces
94	  an existential domain by collecting the constraints that keep it from being

96	  invariance: with `ArrayList` extending `List` and both invariant, subtypes

100	- **Not argued.** The paper argues that the rule is sufficient, not that it

104	
105	- **Subtyping.** Declaration-site variance on trait type parameters, as in
106	  the example "T⟦U2, U1, U1⟧ <: T⟦U1, U2, U1⟧" for `trait T⟦+P, -Q, =S⟧` with

108	- **Positions.** [D-Method] checks that covariant and contravariant class

112	  parameters of traits are invariant" (pp. 11:11-12).
113	- **The overloading rules do not change.** "The overloading rules for FGF

118	  type-sound manner requires keeping track of the static types of method

134	## 4. How dispatch picks among overloads
135	
136	### 4.1 The static rules (§4, pp. 11:12-15)
137	
138	- **The reading of a generic declaration.** Following Allen et al. 2011, a
139	  generic declaration is "a single declaration whose domain type is
140	  existentially quantified over its type parameters", not "a set of
141	  infinitely many monomorphic declarations" (p. 11:3). "A monomorphic method
142	  declaration is a generic method declaration without any type parameter"
143	  (p. 11:5).
144	- **Specificity.** The informal rules compare applicable sets, "which is not
145	  practically checkable", so the formal ones compare domain types by
146	  subtyping (p. 11:12). This is sound but "not complete" (p. 11:13), and
147	  existential reduction narrows the gap (§2 above).
148	- **Three rules for every pair of same-named declarations** (Fig. 5,
149	  p. 11:13):
150	  - No Duplicates: the two domains are not each below the other; either
151	    [No-Dup-Not-Less] or [No-Dup-Not-Gtr] suffices, so the rule refuses
152	    exactly a pair whose domains are mutual subtypes (p. 11:12).
153	  - Meet: the domains exclude ([Meet-Excl], their intersection reduces to
154	    `Bottom`), or one is below the other, or a third declaration's domain is
155	    equivalent to their intersection ([Meet-Third]).
156	  - Return Type ([Return-Test]): when d1 is more specific than d2,
157	    `arrow(d1)` must be a subtype of `∀⟦κ, κ′⟧((α ⊓ α′) → ρ′)`, where the
158	    κ are both declarations' type parameters, α and α′ their domains and ρ′
159	    the less specific return type.
160	- **What [Return-Test] guarantees.** It checks the informal rule "for any
161	  instance of d2 instantiated with σ2 that is applicable to γ, there exists
162	  an instance of d1 … that is applicable to γ and has a return type that is
163	  a subtype of the return type of the instance of d2" (p. 11:15). That is,
164	  it quantifies over every instance of the less specific declaration.
165	- **Theorem 4.1** (p. 11:15). "For any method invocation, there always
166	  exists a unique most specific method declaration in its set of applicable
167	  method declarations." No Duplicates makes specificity antisymmetric, and
168	  the Meet Rule gives "a meet for every nonempty subset".
169	- **Static resolution** ([T-Method], [MSAV], Fig. 7, p. 11:16). The checker
170	  picks an instance of the most specific declaration applicable to the static
171	  argument types, and annotates the call with that instance's return type.
172	  The type-annotated expression `ϵ.m(ϵ): α` is what runs.
173	
174	### 4.2 The dynamic choice (§5.2, pp. 11:16-21)
175	
176	- **The contract.** "dynamic overloading resolution then must select an
177	  instance of the most specific method declaration that is applicable to the
178	  dynamic types of the arguments and whose return type is a subtype of the
179	  static type of the expression" (p. 11:15).
180	- **Types at run time.** Types are reified: "all the type parameters are
181	  instantiated with ground types at run time", and a value's run-time type is
182	  its *ilk* (p. 11:17). Ground types include unions and intersections
183	  (Fig. 8, p. 11:17).
184	- **[R-Method]** (p. 11:17). It sorts the visible declarations most-to-least
185	  specific ("This order is statically determinable, so the sorting can be
186	  done at compile time"). It then runs the *dispatch semipredicate* on each
187	  declaration in turn and takes the first that succeeds. The receiver's ilk is
188	  matched together with the arguments' ilks, which is what makes the dispatch
189	  symmetric.
190	- **The semipredicate** ([Dispatch], pp. 11:17-18) has three steps:
191	  1. match the argument ilks against the domain to get lower and upper bounds
192	     for the method type parameters;
193	  2. match the call's static return type against the declared return type to
194	     get bounds "to make sure that the dynamic dispatch preserves type";
195	  3. solve the bounds.
196	
197	  "If any of these steps fails, the semipredicate is false: the declaration
198	  is not applicable" (p. 11:18). Matching a union can yield several candidate
199	  bound lists, combined as a Cartesian product (pp. 11:18-19).
200	- **Solving** (Fig. 10, p. 11:19). The rule works from the rightmost type
201	  parameter to the left and "computes a substitution … by taking the
202	  intersection of the upper bounds", declared and computed. It then
203	  propagates the choice into the declared lower bounds of the parameters to
204	  its left. It "never instantiates method type parameters with Bottom". The
205	  right-to-left pass works because of the binding restrictions (p. 11:11):
206	  - a method type parameter's scope "extends to the right of its
207	    declaration";
208	  - "no reference to a method type parameter appears in any of the upper
209	    bounds";
210	  - the union of the lower bounds must be below the intersection of the upper
211	    bounds.
212	- **The worked example** (§5.2.4, pp. 11:20-21).
213	  - Two covariant `append` declarations, over `SortedList` and over `List`.
214	  - The call has static type `List⟦C3⟧` and argument ilks `SortedCons⟦C1⟧`

216	  - The `SortedList` declaration fails on the second argument, so the `List`

218	  - So the instance comes from the static return type's upper bound, not from
219	    the ilks' C1 and C2.
220	- **Why intersection of upper bounds.** The Fortress team "had assumed …
221	  that once the tightest possible upper and lower bounds for a method type
222	  parameter have been found, then the union (or pseudo-union) of the lower
223	  bounds should be chosen". For that and for a hybrid "we were unable to
224	  complete the proofs of correctness", so the algorithm "always chooses the
225	  intersection of the upper bounds" (p. 11:25).
226	- **Union instances.** A type parameter can be instantiated at a union at
227	  run time. In the paper's example `O.m(3, true): (Int ⊔ Boolean)`, "P of m
228	  is inferred as (Int ⊔ Boolean) by the dispatch semipredicate at run time"
229	  (p. 11:21).

305	    efficient dispatch (`static.tick:83-89`);
306	  - ilks;
307	  - the most-to-least-specific order with a first-success scan of dispatch
308	    semipredicates (`dispatch.tick:5-20`);
309	  - right-to-left processing of type parameters under left-to-right scoping
310	    (`dispatch.tick:67`).
311	- *The differences:*
312	  - **Inputs to dispatch.** Welterweight dispatches on the ilks alone: it is
313	    "possible to select the dynamically most specific applicable function or
314	    method from an overload set using only the ilks of the argument values; no
315	    other information about the arguments is needed" (`evaluation.tick:30-33`).
316	    POPL adds the call's static return type.
317	  - **The instance.** Welterweight aims at "the most specific instantiation"
318	    by propagating lower limits (`dispatch.tick:67`). It leaves the Return
319	    Type Rule to "one final adjustment step … after the entrypoint [has] been
320	    chosen", with no static type to adjust to (`dispatch.tick:212`). POPL
321	    takes the intersection of the upper bounds, the static return type among
322	    them.
323	  - **Proof.** Welterweight states soundness as propositions that "should
324	    also hold" if "our type system is sound" (`evaluation.tick:71-99`). POPL
325	    proves them.
326	  - **Language.** Welterweight's is larger: top-level functions, a typecase
327	    (`R-Match-Succeeds`), `comprises` and `excludes` clauses, and coverage of
328	    abstract declarations. POPL drops all of these. POPL does handle
329	    contravariance and intersections in matching, where Welterweight's main
330	    algorithm is "Simplified version: no contravariance or ∩", with
331	    contravariance a variation (`dispatch.tick:62`, `:365`).
332	  - **Self types.** Welterweight's self-typed-generics dispatch step is
333	    commented out (`dispatch.tick:195-210`); POPL has no self types at all.
334	
335	**Naden, "The Return Type Rule and Generics"** (2012-08-31,
336	`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex`).
337	- *Rejected:* letting the static context limit which definitions are
338	  applicable, so that overloads failing the Return Type Rule could pass.
339	  "By adding contextual information to the concept of the overload set, we
340	  muddy its semantics" (`:241-305`, quoted at `:289-290`).
341	- *Kept:* the Return Type Rule, plus multiple instantiation exclusion: "any
342	  type which is a subtype of two distinct instantiations of a single generic
343	  type is equivalent to Bottom" (`:342-347`), with a proof (`:433`).
344	- *Why:* a canonical instance for run-time choice (`headOrID`, "Context
345	  does not give us any clue", `:480-495`). So "Fortress implements blanket
346	  multiple instantiation exclusion" (`:496`).
347	- *For covariant parameters:* a minimal instance suffices, "the ancestor
348	  meet rule that appears in the failed OOPSLA 2012 submission" (`:512-538`).
349	  He adds a second, cross-instantiation restriction between a covariant
350	  subtrait and its supertrait (`:540-566`). He finds that the numeric tower's
351	  self-type idiom breaks it, and that "more work needs to be done"
352	  (`:568-633`). His suggested rewrite puts the self type in a bound,
353	  `add⟦X <: Ring⟦X⟧⟧(X, X): X` (`:620-624`).
354	
355	**Naden, "Enforcing Fortress' Return Type Rule at Runtime"** (2012-08-31,
356	`Papers/RuntimeInstantiation/RTRinstantionTheory.tex`, with the notes of
357	May to July 2012 beside it).
358	- *Proposed:* adding bounds from the call's static return type to run-time
359	  instantiation "without changing which function definition will be chosen"
360	  (`:73-80`).
361	- *Proved:* a theorem that under the Return Type Rule the return-type bounds
362	  are satisfiable exactly when applicability is, so they can join the
363	  single pass (`:279-298`).
364	- *Not done:* the bound-generation algorithm and the open coding (`:84-89`).
365	
366	**POPL 2019 against these.**
367	- It carries out the second write-up in a full calculus, with proofs: the
368	  return-type bounds in the semipredicate, and Lemmas 5.8 and 5.9.
369	- It stays within the first write-up's position: overload sets are validated
370	  statically and without context, the Return Type Rule is kept, and the
371	  exclusion rule is kept with the covariant relaxation, extended to
372	  contravariance.
373	- It does not do what that write-up rejected: the static type chooses the
374	  instance, never the declaration (§5 above). One part of Naden's objection
375	  still applies to the instance: which instance runs depends on static
376	  information (the `append` example).
377	- It has no counterpart to the cross-instantiation restriction. Whether
378	  [Return-Test] refuses Naden's `coTail` pair instead has not been worked
379	  out here.
380	- It says nothing on the tower problem.
381	- It excludes the F-bounded method parameters of Naden's suggested rewrite
382	  (§6).

385	
386	- **Instantiation exclusion and route A (POSITIONS 2026-09-24).**
387	  - [Anc-Same-Trait] is the rule route A keeps: blanket for invariant
388	    parameters, as rung S states it in Luchangco's two-part form
389	    (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick:353-360`).
390	  - For covariant parameters the two are consistent by our reading: the
391	    Types chapter lets two instances share a value unless their covariant
392	    arguments exclude, and the paper asks a class with both to have an
393	    instance below both. The Types chapter has only `covariant`; the paper
394	    also has contravariance.
395	  - The record summarises the route as "culminating in the POPL 2019 paper,
396	    which keeps the rule and specialisation by a run-time return-type check,
397	    with no self types and no tower". The full text bears that out (§§2, 5,
398	    6).
399	  - The paper uses the rule inside the overloading check (existential
400	    reduction, pp. 11:13-14). That is the same work instantiation exclusion
401	    does in the checker's domain reduction
402	    (`reviews/overloading-judgement.md` § 3.5).
403	  - **[repo]** The rule was in the checker from 2010 (FACTS, the exclusion
404	    fork, dated). The paper's 2012 date is for the ancestor form.
405	- **Answer 9's overloading rules (POSITIONS 2026-09-26).**
406	  - The paper is answer 9's model, formalised and proved: existential
407	    domains, the plain declaration as the degenerate case, the three rules,
408	    and specificity by domain subtyping (§4.1).
409	  - Calls write no static arguments (Fig. 2). So answer 9's positional rule,
410	    which exists for calls that do, has no counterpart. That fits answer 9's
411	    note on the 2011 paper.
412	  - The paper overloads methods only. Fortress's top-level functions and
413	    operators are, by our reading, the receiver-free case.
414	- **The return-type rule over every instance (answer 9, defect 2).**
415	  [Return-Test] is exactly the construction answer 9 prescribes for the
416	  checker rung, the "special arrow" `∀[Δ1, Δ2] (S1 ∩ S2) → T2` with the less
417	  specific declaration's parameters kept quantified
418	  (`reviews/overloading-judgement.md` § 3.5). The paper states that it
419	  covers every instance of the less specific declaration (p. 11:15), and
420	  its universal reduction is the paper's form of "except where the domain
421	  reduction forces an equality" (pp. 11:14-15). The rung can cite Fig. 5 and
422	  Fig. 6 as its specification.
423	- **Run-time instantiation of a dispatched generic (item 30, POSITIONS
424	  2026-09-29).** The decision: the generic declaration runs, at the instance
425	  the value fixes, and at the least instance within the bounds where it fixes
426	  none; Naden's return-type restriction is future work
427	  (`reviews/plain-beside-generic-judgement.md:74`, `:159`).
428	  - *Which declaration:* the paper agrees. The most specific declaration
429	    applicable to the ilks runs (Lemma 5.9).
430	  - *Naden's restriction:* the paper is its published, proved form (§§5, 7).
431	  - *The instance where the value does not fix it:* the paper diverges. It
432	    takes the intersection of the upper bounds, declared and from the static
433	    return type (p. 11:19), and reports that the least instance, the union
434	    of the lower bounds, could not be proved correct (p. 11:25). Item 30's
435	    default is Welterweight's "most specific instantiation"
436	    (`dispatch.tick:67`), which is that unproved choice.
437	  - *Where the value fixes it* (an invariant position), the two agree.
438	  - *An example* (ours, by reading, not run): `wrap[\X extends Number\](x:
439	    X): Box[\X\]` beside `wrap(a: Any): Any` is a valid pair (the generic is
440	    more specific, and its return type is below `Any`). Called through a
441	    variable of type `Any` holding a `ZZ32`, item 30's default runs it at
442	    `ZZ32` and returns a `Box[\ZZ32\]`. The paper's rule runs it at `Number`,
443	    the declared bound, since the static return type `Any` adds nothing, and
444	    returns a `Box[\Number\]`.
445	  - *Unions:* the paper also instantiates at run-time unions (p. 11:21),
446	    which the compiled path does not have (item 30's judgement, line 74).
447	  - Both points should reach the coordinator before batch 7b's rung S writes
448	    item 30's sentence.
449	- **The `covariant` keyword (row 404, POSITIONS 2026-09-26).**
450	  - FGFV is the formal account of the 2012 `covariant` and `contravariant`
451	    modifiers: position checks, the ancestor rule relaxed by variance, and

453	  - It also says what carrying variance to run time takes beyond

456	  - It is the design reference for worklist item 12 when that is taken up.

462	  - The paper has no closed types, so it says nothing on reading a
463	    `comprises` clause, and its "obvious" addition is not shown.

3	# Where the design intent is written down
4	
5	The specification says what the language is, not why; the why sits in five places, and this file says which place holds which area.
6	
7	The five places: `Papers/` (five in-repo paper directories, four of them buildable); the Guy Steele corpus indexed by `research/README.md` (links, plus per-session local copies under the gitignored `research/decks/`); `research/extracts/` (our committed working notes on those sources); the specification's own draft-only apparatus (the `\note{}` boxes and the Internal Document appendix, both suppressed in release builds); and the source tree itself (tool docs, long design comments, aspirational test directories, commit messages).
8	
9	Two structural facts to carry into the rest of this file.
10	
11	The rationale that is in the specification is in the *draft* build only: `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex:24-37` defines `\note` as empty when `\release` is set, and `Specification/appendices/appendices.tex:24-26` includes the Internal Document chapter only in the non-release build; "Internal Document" appears 0 times in the text of the published `Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf` and twice in the in-repo draft render `Specification/fortress.pdf` (599 pages), which also carries 36 occurrences of the editorial "Victor:" notes that the 1.0 PDF has none of.

There are three reasons: for some, no declaration of `Integral` applies to a sibling type even with coercion; for others, the declarations that apply by coercion tie; and a getter must be the type's own member. Each integer type declares its own comparisons, `CMP`, `MAXNUM` and `MINNUM`, and a `^` with an `IntLiteral` exponent. Without them, a typed integer with a numeral operand ties between a declaration inherited from a generic trait and the same operator's own declarations in `ZZ64`, `QQ` and `RR64`. The rung also made `MatchFailure` an unchecked exception: it extends `UncheckedException` (row 590). The sites that it left have rows (report section 5). Limit: under walk the name `IntLiteral` also denotes a value, a zero that no numeral reaches, and its arithmetic answers a `ZZ32` against its declared `IntLiteral` (row 578). F-263 holds the integer powers' types, and F-255 `List`'s ordering. Gated under walk by `tests/NumberOrderListDeclarations.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-number-order-slips/REPORT.md` sections 1, 4 and 5.

Walk checks such overloads against the library's only on a cold cache (F-269). So a pass of that test shows that they coexist with the library only if the run started from an empty cache. Detail: `reviews/library-scalar-extension-review.md`, change 1.

Each wider integer type converts from each narrower one, and `RR64` from a `ZZ32` and an `IntLiteral`; a `ZZ64` goes into `RR64` only when written out (P-74). `QQ` converts from the five integer types and `IntLiteral`, and `RR64` converts from `RR32` too (F-139). `NN32` does not yet convert into `RR64`: P-75 decides that it will. `Number`'s `=` compares a float with an exact number after `asFloat`, so it is not transitive (row 434). In the interpreter's library, a range that reaches `ZZ32`'s minimum or maximum has the right size and elements, with no overflow, unless it is strided and a difference of its bounds leaves `ZZ32` (row 522, below). On the compiled path, the compiler library has no strided range (row 514), and its range `IN` and `=` are always `false` (rows 479, 481). The rule does not reach these open defects: a big operator over a list of numerals with no static argument (row 432); a `nat` parameter used as a value at an `NN32` binding, refused at the binding (row 486); a static argument that only the call's result mentions, at a typed binding (row 510); and a varargs or tuple parameter over mixed widths (row 511). Gated by `tests/InferCoercionRungK.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/REPORT.md` sections 2 and 9.

Each type also declares its own `MAXNUM` and `MINNUM`. Under walk an `NN32` operator with a numeral answers a `ZZ64` (row 484). Compiled, `NN32` with `ZZ32` or `ZZ64` answers `ZZ` (row 442). Gated by `tests/IntegerMinMaxRungM.fss` and `IntegerMaxNumMinNum.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-integer-minmax/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 9.
- F-141 **Under `walk`, a type parameter that nothing at a call fixes takes its declared bound, and a lone one with no narrowest candidate takes its bound where every argument is below it.** It builds P-48. A lone type parameter is one that is the whole declared type of some argument and that no other argument fixes (F-137); where some argument is not below its bound, it takes the arguments' join. A type parameter that the declared parameter types mention only in function domains, an odd number of arrows deep and never inside a static argument, as `T` in `g: T -> ZZ32`, is bounded by the arguments only from above. Where nothing bounds it from below, it takes the meet of its declared bound and the bounds that the arguments place on it. An F-bounded parameter stays open (F-143). A reduction or comprehension that writes no static argument fixes its big operator's parameter by the declared type of its value, else by its elements' join (F-228). That rule is the coordinator's call. Two more rules are defaults of the walk-instance rung's decision record. First, a parameter that only another fixed parameter's bound mentions takes that parameter's instance, not its own bound: `ap[\T, A extends T\](a: A)` gives `T` the type of `a` (D3, row 592). Gated by `tests/Infer*Walk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-instance/REPORT.md` section 2 and its `decision-record.md` section 2; `compile-ladder/rung-walk-elements/REPORT.md` section 1; `compile-ladder/rung-walk-meet/REPORT.md` section 1.

The open type, printed `OPEN`, is below every type, and every value matches it. A reduction or a comprehension that writes no static argument is first instantiated by its declared type or by its elements' join (F-228). So the open parameter reaches one only where neither fixes it: an empty `SUM` or `PROD` that no declared type directs, which takes `ZZ32`'s identity whatever its body's type (row 716), or a clause form whose declared type or join does not fit the bound (F-228).
