Where overloads are compared, a tuple, arrow or generic type that holds the open type admits no more than it would at `BottomType`: beside `pick(x: Any)`, `pick(x: (T,T))` does not take `(1, 2)`, though a lone `one(x: (T,T))` does (row 663, contested). In a probe by the rung's skeptic, the agent that checks a rung's work after its worker, a method declared over `T` in an object whose `T` stayed open was the most specific one, and so was chosen for every argument; no gated test holds this. Gated by `tests/InferUnfixedFBoundedWalk.fss` and `OpenTupleDispatchWalk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-open-param/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 11; its `SKEPTIC.md` section 3, finding 3 (the probe).
- F-151 **In the interpreter's library, `Vector`, `Matrix` and their factories and operators bound their element type by `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }`.** `Number` declares no arithmetic, so the compiled checker accepts the bodies' arithmetic only through `MultiplicativeRing[\T\]`. `Number` stays in the bound because its `comprises` clause lists every type below it, so an element type excludes `String`; the ring alone does not give that. That exclusion makes the four juxtapositions of a vector or a matrix with a scalar `T`, in either order, a valid overloading beside the library's juxtapositions with a `String`. `Number` also declares the `asFloat` that the vector norm calls. The eight number types meet the bound. `Number` itself and the numeral type `IntLiteral` do not, since neither is a ring at its own type. So `Vector[\Number,n\]` is not a well-formed type, and `array1` and `array2` have no branch for `Number`: called at `Number`, they give a plain array at run time, not a vector or a matrix (F-229). The checker accepts a call whose argument's type is built from the caller's own type parameter under the same bound, such as the norm's `squaredNorm(me)` (F-227). The scalar extension, the eight operators between an array and a scalar, has bounds of its own, also with `Number` (F-119). Gated under walk by `tests/ArrayElementAlgebra.fss`. The bound is the default that `reviews/array-fork2-judgement.md` recommended. It landed when the curator said to land it. Detail: that judgement, sections 2.5 (what `Number`'s `comprises` clause gives), 2.9, way 3 (the ring alone, measured) and 4 (the bound and its cost).
- F-152 **`Vector` and `Matrix` are the only array traits with an algebra, `AdditiveGroup`, and their element must be a `Number`.** They inherit `+`, `-`, unary `-` and `zero`, and nothing from another algebraic trait. `Array3` has no algebra (row 292). `×` reaches no array, by design: juxtaposition is the inner product (rows 109, 293). Walk accepts, unchecked, a carrier that extends both `Matrix` and `MultiplicativeRing`, and its `+` then fails (row 371). The specification's `T^n` denotes these traits (row 24), and neither path takes it. Detail: `reviews/array-design-ways.md` section 2.
- F-225 **In a self-typed trait with no `comprises` clause, or one that lists only `...`, the compiled checker types `self` in the method bodies as `C[\X\] & X`, the trait met with the implementing type, read from the trait's F-bound; the methods' signatures keep `self` at the plain trait type `C[\X\]`, and the checker refuses an extender at another type.** It builds P-146. A self-typed trait is a trait `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`. The checker also takes a parameter bounded by a self-typed trait that the trait extends at that parameter, as the team's `Containment` mixins are: a default of the coordinator's. In a trait whose `comprises` clause lists types, `self` is instead the trait met with the union of those types. For example, `object Bad extends Integral[\ZZ32\]` is refused, since `Bad` is not a `ZZ32`. The rule accepts every self-typed body of the library but `Integral`'s `numerator`, which each integer type declares instead (P-146). When it landed, the distance stage's self-type class fell from 29 errors to 0 (the distance from 85 to 55), one measurement on that tree. Walk has no such rule and loads what it refuses. A compiled default body that returns `self` dies at class load with a `VerifyError` when the trait's self-type parameter is an object type, as in `object Pt(…) extends Shape[\Pt\]`: an open defect (row 695). The rule refuses, rightly, two team declarations, each an open row: the demo `trips.fss`'s `generator` (row 710) and `PureList`'s `List` (row 355). Gated by `compiler_tests/SelfType*` and `XXXSelfType*`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-self-type/REPORT.md` sections 1, 2, 4 and 7.
- F-227 **The compiled checker replaces a closed trait among an intersection's conjuncts by those of its listed types that no other conjunct excludes, only where that excluding conjunct names no type variable or inference variable, so `K ∩ R[\T\]` stays as written; below a union, an inference variable takes the whole union as one upper bound, and a type variable is tried through its bound as well as against each member.** The code is `normConjunct` and, for the union cases, `pSubInner`, in `scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala`. So a call through a parameter bounded by a closed trait and a bound that excludes one of its listed types checks, and a generic declaration so bounded, beside a declaration on the closed trait, is a valid overloading (rows 686, 687, 689, 690 and 711). A call whose argument's type only carries the parameter, `Box[\T\]`, under a ground second bound, stays refused: an open defect (row 712). Before the checker kept such an intersection as written, it accepted, through the expansion, an overloading that it now refuses, on a question that Appendix I lists as not settled (row 713, contested; `compiler_tests/XXXOverloadTwoBoundsClosedTraitExclusion` pins the refusal). Gated by `compiler_tests/*TwoBoundsClosedTrait` and `*TwoGroundBounds*ClosedTrait`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-checker-bounds/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 6.

content.content:
- F-166 **On the topics of its Types chapter, such as the exclusion rule and covariance, the team's latest word is the unfinished restart, not `Specification/`.** The restart, `Documentation/Specification/`, was never adopted. Its Types chapter restates the exclusion rule as "instantiation exclusion" and adds `covariant`. On the rest of static parameters, and on traits beyond a stub, exceptions, components and the numeric library, `Specification/` is the only statement. Which text governs is the curator's: `Specification/` stays the standard, the Types chapter is cited beside it, and `covariant` is future work (P-25). The type group's POPL 2019 paper is later than both (F-271). Detail: `coordinator/spec-lineage.md` section 6 and its "Coordinator's check (2026-09-26)".
- F-167 **The specification states instantiation exclusion and keeps each example that the rule refuses, marked "Not allowed"; the calculi of Appendix A carry a callout that they predate the rule.** It builds P-97. It also bars a `where`-clause variable from an `extends` clause's static arguments. The covariance example, the empty list, the empty optional value and the root type `Object`'s algebraic supertraits each stand beside the library's shape, which runs on both paths except `Nothing[\String\]` on the compiled prelude (row 331). A subtrait of every instantiation stays as the counterexample that introduces the rule, and the internal appendix's refused examples get a callout each. The checker does not yet refuse two cases: an object that extends two instantiations that differ only in a `bool` argument (row 406), and one that extends two instantiations of one trait where one instantiation's argument is the object's own static parameter, such as `O[\nat n\] extends { Vec[\n\], Vec[\3\] }` (row 414). Detail and examples: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md` sections 2 and 3; its section 4.2 (the calculi's callout).
- F-168 **The specification's number chapters describe the flat library, and its advanced chapter on rational quantities stays word for word under a callout that marks it superseded.** The eight number types are siblings under `Number` (F-131). They convert by the library's coercions (P-74), and every other conversion is explicit, such as `asFloat(x)`. The sign-refined types, such as positive ℚ, are gone; a program tests a value's sign at run time (P-80). ℚ holds +∞, −∞ and 0/0, and claims neither a field nor a total order. `QQ` extends the four algebraic traits that the library declares on it, `StandardPartialOrder`, `StandardMinMax`, `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`, and their laws hold for the finite rationals. F-172 gives the integer chapter's rules. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-numbers/decision-record.md` section 3; `Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex:224-229` (ℚ's traits); `Specification/advanced-lib/numbers-advanced.tex:14` (the callout).
- F-169 **The Working Draft never wrote static-argument inference, never named the type that a library gives an integer numeral, and never named a range's integer type; the specification's text on these is the revival's.** The Working Draft's inference chapter is a heading and notes. It described numeral types, such as `NaturalNumeral[\n,10,v\]`, and said that libraries define coercions from numerals to integers and rationals. But a note of its own leaves the numeral types' hierarchy undescribed, and it names no type that a library declares for a numeral. Its ranges section names no integer type. The later restart adds nothing on the three. So a citation of the specification on them cites the revival, not the team. The revised text states F-173's inference rule and F-170's ranges, and gives an integer numeral the type `IntLiteral` (P-76). Detail: `reviews/numerics-plan-coordinator/evidence-B.md` sections 1 and 2; `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:87-96` and `:132-148` (the note and the coercions); `Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:154-156` (the callout on the numeral types).
- F-171 **The specification reads a `comprises` clause as the restart's Types chapter does: every value of the trait is a value of a listed type.** So a trait or object that extends the closed trait must be below a listed type, with two exceptions. A trait with a `comprises` clause of its own may stay unlisted if each of its own listed types is below a listed type of the closed trait. A trait with static parameters may stay unlisted if at least one type extends it and every type that extends it is below a listed type. A listed type may be an instantiation at the trait's static parameters or `where`-clause variables. The text does not say whether a bare type variable may be listed; walk overflows its stack on one (row 407). The compiled checker departs in three ways: it checks only the closed trait's immediate subtypes (row 487), it reads the clause in the subtrait's own type-variable names (row 489), and it finds extenders by the simple text of a name (row 490). Whether the team's commented `comprises Integral[\I\] where [\I\]` is valid is open (F-121). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-comprises/decision-record.md` section 2; `Specification/basic/traits.tex:235-258`.
- F-173 **The specification's type-inference chapter states the rule that the compiled checker builds: the declaration is chosen first, then its static arguments are inferred.** It states P-46, P-48 and P-49. A type parameter that a parameter's declared type mentions inside another type, as `List[\T\]` mentions `T`, is fixed by the argument at that position. One that is the whole declared type of one or more parameters, as `T` is of `x: T`, and that nothing else fixes, takes the narrowest type, within its bounds, that every one of those arguments has or converts into: `ZZ64` for a `ZZ32` and an `NN32`. Where there is none, and no numeral settles the tie, it takes its bound, narrowed by what the call's expected type requires of the return type (P-48). So does a type parameter that neither an argument nor the expected type fixes. Inference never gives a type parameter `BottomType`. The compiled path departs from the chapter in these ways, among others. It bounds a type parameter written without an `extends` clause by `Object`, not `Any`, as the chapter's callouts say (row 412, P-42). Its prelude lacks the coercion of `NN32` into `ZZ64`, so a `ZZ32` and an `NN32` instantiate a type parameter at `ZZ`, not `ZZ64`; no callout names this (row 442, `compiler_tests/XXXInferPromoteNN32`). The callouts at `Specification/basic/inference.tex:236-298` and `:364-425` also give walk's departures, such as the return type `BottomType` that walk gives a function expression that declares none (row 587). Plain tests gate the rule for a type parameter that is a parameter's whole type, at its bound where no argument type is narrowest, on both paths: `compiler_tests/InferLone*` and `tests/InferLone*Walk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-instance-bound/REPORT.md` (the bound rule); `Specification/basic/inference.tex:47-124` (the chapter's rule).
- F-174 **The specification states the type group's 2011 overloading model: declarations of one name may differ in their static parameters, and a declaration with static parameters is read as one declaration over all its instances within its bounds.** It states P-45 and P-42. The section "Declarations with Static Parameters" states the OOPSLA 2011 paper's three rules: No Duplicates, Return Type and Meet. It gives one more restriction as the compiled path's, not the language's. Where one generic declaration is more specific than another with as many static parameters, the two must declare them of the same kinds, position by position. Also, the more specific one's return type must be a subtype of the other's when their static parameters are matched by position, so the checker refuses an override whose return type reorders its static parameters (row 398, fixed). The section "Principles of Overloading" forbids overloading a functional whose single parameter's type is a type parameter with the bound `Any` written, as `T extends Any`. A type parameter with no `extends` clause, whose bound is also `Any`, is exempt. Both paths refuse such an overload: the checker in `OverloadingChecker.checkBoundAny`, and walk since row 534's fix. Neither path runs every set that the rules allow. Appendix I's entry "Overloading with static parameters" names the sets that each path fails. In row 542, the checker refuses a generic declaration beside a plain one over an object type, as `ident[\T\](x: T): T` beside `ident(x: Circle): Circle`. In row 537, the code generator fails on two generic declarations whose bounds differ. In row 539, walk refuses at load the 2019 paper's valid set over an array list and a list. In rows 779 and 780, walk fails on two generic functional methods one of whose declared domains lies inside the other's: in a trait or object without static parameters it refuses them at load, and in a trait with static parameters it loads them, but a call to which both apply fails. Detail: `Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:134-150` and `:531-674`; `compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md` sections 3 and 4.
- F-175 **The specification reads a `comprises` clause at the level of values in every passage.** It builds P-60. Appendix I's entry "Traits with comprises clauses read at the level of values" records the change. A call whose argument's static type stands between two closed traits runs the declaration that covers its value. Where its declarations have no static parameters, its type is the intersection of its most specific declarations' return types. Appendix I names five places where the compiled path departs. The checker checks a `comprises` clause at the closed trait's immediate subtypes only (row 487). The code generator crashes on a method call on a result typed by that intersection (row 540). Where any declaration of the overload set has static parameters, the checker types such a call by one of its most specific declarations instead, a deliberate choice (row 543). The checker refuses the Meet Rule's example for closed traits when its declarations have static parameters (row 546). The checker's verdict on an overload set can depend on the components compiled before it in the same JVM (row 547). Detail: `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:3185-3240`, with the rows at `:1597-1606` and `:3446-3459`; `compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md` sections 8 and 9.
- F-223 **The specification's No Duplicates Rule is the papers' non-strict rule, and the compiled checker applies it, to functional methods wherever their `self` parameters stand, abstract ones included.** Two declarations of one name may not each be applicable to every call to which the other is, as in the type group's papers of 2011 and 2019 (P-26). The checker refuses such a pair, two functional methods at different `self` positions and an abstract functional method beside a concrete one among them: "There are multiple declarations of f with the same parameter type", naming the domain of the declaration written first. It checks no symbolic operator (row 584); such a pair passes it and stops the code generator (row 726). Walk refuses at load such a pair of two generic declarations whose parameter types mention their static parameters, as `dup[\T\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `dup[\U\](x: Box[\U\])`; it refuses too a generic declaration beside one whose parameter types are its bounds, a plain one or a generic one whose parameter types mention none of its static parameters, 'fails because their parameter lists have the same types'. Gated by `compiler_tests/XXXNoDuplicatesRule`, `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleSelfPositions`, `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleSelfPositionsPlain`, `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleAbstract` and `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleAbstractSelfPositions`, the checker's departure by `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleSelfPositionsOperator`, walk's refusal by `tests/NoDuplicatesRuleWalk`, and those two refusals by `tests/GenericBesidePlainSameDomain` and `GenericBesideGenericSameDomain`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-popl-examples/REPORT.md` section 4, its `SKEPTIC.md` section 2, `compile-ladder/rung-duplicates-coverage/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 8, and `compile-ladder/rung-checker-abstract-callsite/REPORT.md` section 1.
- F-243 **The 13 errors that were filed as waiting on `where` clauses, 13 of the distance's 49 at the gates of climb batches 15b and 16, are all cleared; the 13th, the list comparisons' site, by conditional extension.** The where-clauses probe traced each of them (A.1). The method condition and the generic `distribute` clear the fusion pairs' 6 (F-242). `AnyList`'s `comprises { List[\E\] } where [\E\]` clause, a comment of the team's made live, clears its 4, with its bodies respelled within `AnyList` and none moved into `List` (F-251). A `cast` at `additiveIdentity`'s and `multiplicativeIdentity`'s fallbacks, `else => 0` and `else => 1`, clears 2 (row 436). Conditional extension cleared the list comparisons' site (the list half of row 634; its tuple half was built earlier), with `ZeroIndexed[\E\]` and an element-wise `=` kept outside the condition (F-255). By the probe, library edits with no new language would also have cleared 12: dropping the fusion pairs, moving `AnyList`'s bodies into `List`, and the `cast` at the fallbacks. Detail: `perf-probes/where-clauses/REPORT.md` A.0, A.1, A.4, B.0 and B.3; `reviews/batch-17-review.md`, section 2.
- F-245 **Checking symbolic operators for overloading adds 186 errors to the distance in the compiled checker, measured at `d97001d19`, whose code is climb batch 20's gate, with crashes caught per name: 54 clear by known library fixes, and 132 wait on two designs that the curator decides.** As the stage runs, the 186 are 185 errors and three crashes on `||`, in `List`'s api and component and `String`'s component, "E is not in the kind env": a checker crash that no fix or design clears (`perf-probes/symbolic-operators-2/REPORT.md` section 1.3). The check was turned on in a copy of the checker whose three loops admit every operator; the checker as built skips them (row 584). The two designs: a bound on the subscripts' index type (124 errors), and a vector plus a number beside a vector plus a vector (8). The probe's candidates S1, an index bound with a rule for tuple indices, and A2, `Vector` and `Matrix` leaving `AdditiveGroup`, clear them with nothing new; A3, the scalar `+` and `-` dropped, also clears the 8. The largest families are the subscripts over a generic `Indexed` (124) and `String`'s four concatenation operators, `||`, `|||`, `//` and `///` (40). An earlier measurement, at `d212b2c1f`, counted 205; batches since cleared `FlatString`'s pair (2; F-259) and 20 of the 21 `^` errors (F-263), and added 3: `|_|` 1 and the scalar `+` and `-` 2. Walk's meet check, which also skips symbolic operators and judges neither `String`'s pairs, the subscripts, `^` nor `=`, refused only `EmptyString`'s `||` when widened the same way in the first probe of these operators. Detail: `perf-probes/symbolic-operators-2/REPORT.md` sections 0 to 2; `perf-probes/symbolic-operators/REPORT.md` section 1.5.
- F-255 **The compiled checker reads conditional extension in its subtype relation: a trait or object that extends a type under a `where` clause that binds no variable and holds trait constraints only is a subtype of that type exactly where the constraints hold.** The `extends` entry itself, an object's value parameters and every member are checked with the constraints holding. The static parameters, the declaration's own `where` clause, its `excludes` and `comprises` clauses and its other `extends` entries are checked without them. The disambiguator drops every trait's and object's `throws` clause and contract, so these are not checked at all (row 781). A clause that binds a variable, or that holds a constraint that is not a trait constraint, is read as before: as a parent at every instance. Limits: a member checked under the condition stays callable where the condition fails (row 773), and walk and the compiled run time read the extension at every instance (row 774). Other readers of the `extends` clause in the checker ignore the condition. Those that go through the type's parents see a conditional parent at no instance: the ancestors (`TypeAnalyzer.ancestors`), which the overloading checker reads to let a concrete method implement an abstract one. Those that read the clause itself see it at every instance: the inherited `excludes` clauses (`TypeAnalyzer.excludesClause`). None of these readers moved a result on the library, and no ledger row holds them (report section 10). In the library, `List` extends `LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\],E\]` only where `E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\]`; its `ZeroIndexed[\E\]` entry and its own element-wise `opr =` stand outside the condition, so every list keeps them (`Library/List.fss:106-107`, `:124-128`). On the rung's own tree, against climb batch 17's gate, this cleared the site `FortressLibrary.fss:2063` and added none. Tests: `compiler_tests/CondExtendChecker`, `XXXCondExtendRefuseChecker`, `XXXCondExtendUnconditionalEntryChecker`, `XXXCondExtendExcludesChecker`, `XXXCondExtendComprisesChecker`, `XXXCondExtendParamBoundChecker`, `XXXCondExtendExcludesWhereChecker`, `CondExtendInheritedMember` (a type that inherits through a conditional parent compiles: the code generator's analyzer reads the parent at every instance), `tests/XXXConditionalExtensionTypeTestWalk`. Detail: `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-checker-conditional-extension/REPORT.md`, sections 1, 6 and 10.
- F-258 **Walk and the compiled checker read exclusion between two declarations, one or both with static parameters, over the whole parameter type, by existential reduction.** A value of both declared domains has, at each position, one instance of each generic type that the two parameter types there are or extend, so those instances' static arguments are equal; the two domains exclude where these equalities cannot hold together, or where, at the instance they force, the parameter types at some position exclude. Walk: the Meet branches of `genericPairValid` and of `validOnDeclaredDomains`'s generic-beside-plain reading also ask `domainsExcludeTogether` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:935` at `a93fb3bfd`), which reads bounds where `mayBeEqual` and `meetParams` read them and reads no `where` clause, varargs or lists of different lengths; at the instance the equalities force, it reads two parameter types that still mention a static parameter apart only where they cannot meet at any instance of it: an object type apart from a type that neither it nor a supertype of it may be, and no `comprises` clause (`excludesAtMeet`, `OverloadedFunction.java:1041` at `84957e6ef`). The checker: `OverloadingOracle.excludes` asks `TypeSchemaAnalyzer.emptyED` beside `subtypeED` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/overloading/OverloadingOracle.scala:326`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeSchemaAnalyzer.scala:444`): the existential reduction's first premise alone, its bounds not read. On the interpreter's library `emptyED` is never reached: `subtypeED` shows all 691 meets the count stage tests empty. The two paths differ on two type parameters whose bounds exclude (row 786); on such a pair one of whose declarations has a `where` clause, which walk refuses and the checker accepts (row 787); and on a pair that walk's parameter check reads apart, reading an object type over a static parameter as excluding a type it is at some instance, as `g[\T\](x: Box[\T\], y: ZZ32)` beside `g(x: Box[\ZZ32\], y: Any)`, which walk loads and the checker refuses (row 788). Gated by `ProjectFortress/tests/GenericPairExcludesTogetherWalk`, `GenericPairForcedObjectApartWalk`, `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/GenericPairExcludesTogether` and `GenericPairSharedSupertypeExclusion` (load, compile and dispatch), and `ProjectFortress/tests/GenericPairFreeArgumentWalk`, `GenericPairObjectSupertypeOverlapWalk` and `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXGenericPairFreeArgument` (refused). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-existential-reduction/REPORT.md` sections 2, 5 and 7.
- F-263 **In the interpreter's library each integer power is declared to answer its base's own type; under walk, at a negative exponent, the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power, a base of 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and any other base raises `IntegerOverflow`.** It builds P-153. Under walk the power answers its base's type and follows these rules at `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64` and `ZZ`, with an exponent of any integer type, including a `ZZ` exponent too large for 64 bits, such as 2^70. Under walk a numeral is a `ZZ32` value (F-74), so `2^(-1)` raises `IntegerOverflow`. `IntLiteral` is the type that the compiled checker gives an integer numeral (F-262). Under walk the name `IntLiteral` also denotes a value, a zero that no numeral reaches. Its power follows the same rules, but answers a `ZZ32`, as all its arithmetic does, against its declared `IntLiteral`: a gap of walk (row 578). `QQ`'s power takes an exponent of any integer type. For a fraction, write a float or rational base: `2.0^(-1)` is 0.5, and `(2/3)^(-1)` is `3/2`. The compiled checker accepts the library's own uses of these powers (the distance stage). microGPT's only integer power is in the library's `strToInt`, always at a nonnegative exponent. The compiled path's own library does not follow these rules. At a negative exponent its `ZZ32` power gives 0 at every base but 0, 1 and -1, and a raw Java `RuntimeException` at a base of 0 (row 441). P-153 lists this, with that power's overflow, which throws a raw Java exception that no Fortress `catch` sees, or saturates quietly (row 523). Tests: `tests/IntegerPowerContractWalk.fss`, `tests/QQPowerExponent.fss`; on the compiled path, the expected failure `compiler_tests/XXXIntegerPowerContractCompiled.test`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-integer-power/REPORT.md` sections 1, 2 and 4 (the change, the tests, the checker's sites); `perf-probes/integer-power/REPORT.md` section 1.6 (microGPT's powers).
- F-265 **No static parameter of the interpreter's library is bounded by `Object`, so no library declaration meets walk's stop on that bound: under walk, an argument whose type is a tuple, `()` or an arrow, at a parameter whose type is a type variable bounded by `Object`, stops the program with an `InterpreterBug`, not a type error (row 471, open).** The stop needs a bound written `Object`, since walk installs a written bound before it unifies the arguments (row 471). The library's result-only parameters are unbounded, as P-48 decides (F-84). Six functions of `FortressLibrary` write the bound `extends Any`, which admits tuples, `()` and arrows: `cast`, `instanceOf`, `identity`, `shared`, `localize` and `copy` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:33-72`; its api declares the first five so, and holds `copy` in a comment). The specification's examples and the compiler tests write `extends Object` (`SpecData/examples/basic/Fun.Decl.fss:19`, `ProjectFortress/other_compiler_tests/Go1a.fss:15`). Row 471 has no test. Evidence: `git grep -nE '\[\\[^\\]*extends +Object' -- Library ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin` prints nothing; walk's stop is from the probe that row 471 records, no longer in the tree. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-result-bounds/REPORT.md` section 10.
- F-270 **The compiled checker opens a value of a trait whose `comprises` clause lists a type at a `where`-clause size: it gives each listed type's `nat` and `int` `where`-clause sizes a fresh name for the call.** In `trait NatParam comprises { N[\n\] } where [\ nat n \]`, a `NatParam` passed where `N[\$n\]` is expected, `$n` being the checker's inference variable for the called function's size parameter, binds `$n` to the fresh size, and the call's result type carries it. An opened size is not known to differ from any size. Walk's `comprises` check at load reads such a size as any size, the same at each of its places; at a call, walk binds the argument's own size. This is way 4a of fork 3 of the array design, a size known only at run time: the checker reads such a size as fixed for that call, not as unknown. P-85 leaves the array design's three questions open with no default; the third stands on this ground, and way 4a is the one way built on it. The code generator does not compile such a trait: "Can't compile TraitDecl NatParamT" (row 307; `compiler_tests/XXXNatOpenRun`). In row 682's program, with `trait NatParamT comprises { Nt[\n\] } where [\nat n\]`, the checker refuses `f(x: NatParamT)` beside `f[\nat n\](x: Nt[\n\])` as two declarations of one parameter type, where walk runs the pair (row 682, contested). F-251 holds the same opening for a type variable. Gated by `compiler_tests/NatOpenChecker`, and under walk by `tests/NatOpenWalk` and `NatOpenUnlistedExtender`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-size-expressions/REPORT.md` section 1, "Fork 3, way 4a, under Q13.3", and section 12.
- F-271 **The type group's POPL 2019 paper gives P-48's instance rule, and its soundness proof does not cover the library's F-bounded functions, such as `SUM` and `BIG MAX`.** By P-48's rule, a type parameter that a call's arguments do not fix takes the intersection of its upper bounds. The paper is later than both the specification and the team's restart (F-166). Its calculus does not let a method type parameter occur in an upper bound, so F-bounded method parameters are outside it. It also leaves out top-level functions and functional methods, among other limits. `reviews/decisions-review/popl-recheck.md` checks the curator's decisions against the paper. Detail: `research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md` sections 6 and 8.
- F-273 **The specification gives the run-time instance of a generic declaration that dispatch reaches, and that the static call did not select, by the POPL 2019 paper's rule.** It builds P-48. A declaration that the static call selected runs at the instance inferred for the call (F-173). Where an argument's value fixes a type parameter, as a value of `Tag[\X\]` fixes `X`, the rule and both paths agree. Where a type parameter is a parameter's whole type, the argument's run-time type only bounds it from below. The rule then gives it its declared bound, narrowed by what the call's static type requires of the return type. The dispatch paragraph's callout says that both paths take the argument's run-time type there instead. Walk always will, since it has no static types (P-48). The compiled path does so because its dispatcher is not given the call's static type (row 538, the expected failure `compiler_tests/XXXGenericInstanceUnfixed`). The callout also says that the compiled path does not yet run the paragraph's second example, a generic declaration beside a plain one, reached through an argument of static type `Any` (row 496). Detail: `Specification/basic/overloading.tex:312-349`, in the chapter "Overloading and Multiple Dispatch"; `compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md` sections 5 and 6.
- F-21 **The February 2011 Working Draft's bare `Nothing`, one object for every `T`, is accepted on neither path: the grammar refuses its `excludes` clause, and without that clause `T` is undefined.** The declaration is `object Nothing extends Maybe[\T\] excludes Just[\T\] where {T extends Object}` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/convenience.tex:40`). Both paths stop at a syntax error at `excludes`, since an object has no `excludes` clause (measured: `reviews/spec-refused-examples.md`, E4). Without that clause, both report `T is undefined` at the `T` of the `extends` clause: a `where` clause on an object binds no type variable of its `extends` clause, as row 17 holds for a trait. Today's specification refuses the form in any case, by instantiation exclusion, and marks it "Not allowed" beside the parametric `Nothing[\T\]` that the interpreter's library writes (F-167). P-90 still calls the bare `Nothing` future work that waits for such `where` clauses, not tried before then. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-maybe/REPORT.md` section 5.
- F-121 **The team's spelling of `AnyIntegral`'s `comprises` clause, `comprises Integral[\I\] where [\I\]`, stays a comment, and no decision says whether it is a valid clause.** The live clause, which lists `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64`, stands (P-44), and the compiled checker accepts it (F-62). The specification lets a listed type hold a `where`-clause variable, at every value of it, and the compiled checker opens such variables, of a `nat`, an `int` or a type (F-146, F-251). Whether the checker accepts the team's spelling on `AnyIntegral` is not measured. Of the team's commented `comprises ... where` clauses, P-151 builds only `AnyList`'s. The comment stays by P-44, which kept it beside the live clause when its `where` form was not built. Whether it becomes live now that the checker opens such variables is an open question, whose default leaves it. content.content:
Given type ${\tt T}\ob{X}$ where $X$ is covariant and type ${\tt S}\ob{Y}$ were $Y$ is covariant and for all $Z$
${\tt S}\ob{Z} <: {\tt T}\ob{Z}$. Let {\tt A} and {\tt B} be distinct ground types where ${\tt A} <: {\tt B}$.  If
$I <: {\tt S}\ob{B}$ and $I <: {\tt T}\ob{A}$, then $I <: {\tt S}\ob{A}$.
\end{quote}

With these two restrictions, we can prove that special case overloads involving covariant type parameters 
will now pass the return type rule as well (TODO).

\subsubsection{Exception for selfless types}

This restriction is problematic for expressing certain types of relationships such as the numeric hierarchy
that is expressed using the so called self-type idiom (now selfless types or trolls). Some sets of numbers
and the operators over them give rise to special algebraic properties known as rings and the more specialized fields.  Fortress
aims to support them in the following way:\\

$\begin{array}{l}
{\bf trait}~{\tt Ring}\ob{X <: {\tt Number}}~{\bf comprises}~X~\dots~{\bf end}\\
{\bf trait}~{\tt Field}\ob{X <: {\tt Number}}~{\bf comprises}~X~{\bf extends}~{\tt Ring}\ob{X}~\dots~{\bf end}
\end{array}$\\

The self-type idiom is realized with the {\bf comprises} clause which contains the instantiation of the self type.
The {\bf comprises} clause limits the types that can extend the given type to those appearing in the clause.
In this idiomatic usage, the type ${\tt Ring}\ob{X}$ is identified as $X$.  Thus a ${\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Q}}$
is really just $\mathbb{Q}$ itself.

Unfortunately, the numerical hierarchy contains crossed instantiations of the kind that we determined
must be outlawed:\\

$\begin{array}{l}
{\bf trait}~\mathbb{Q}~{\bf extends}~{\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Q}}~\ldots~{\bf end}\\
{\bf trait}~\mathbb{Z}~{\bf extends}~\{ \mathbb{Q}, {\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}\}~\ldots~{\bf end}\\
\end{array}$\\

A $\mathbb{Z}$ is a ${\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Q}}$ and a ${\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$ but not
a ${\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$ which breaks our rule given above.  As above, we can come
up with an example that is unsound if we allow this type hierarchy.\\

$\begin{array}{l}
{\it add}\ob{X}({\tt Ring}\ob{X}, {\tt Ring}\ob{X}) :{\tt Ring}\ob{X}~(*){\it def1}\\
{\it add}\ob{Y}({\tt Field}\ob{Y},{\tt Field}\ob{Y}) : {\tt Field}\ob{Y}~(*){\it def2}\\
\end{array}$\\

Take type $\mathbb{Z}$ which is provided as the inputs to {\it add}.  Both {\it def1} and {\it def2}
are applicable.  But if we instantiate {\it def1}
at $\mathbb{Z}$, then we have a return type of ${\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$ for the less specific
definition.  The more specific {\it def2} is only applicable when instantiated at $\mathbb{Q}$, but the
resulting return type ${\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Q}}$ is not a subtype of ${\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$,
thus witnessing the failure of the return type rule.

Recall that the return type rule handles two failure cases: first, the possibility that more specific
type information at runtime will cause a more specific function definition to be chosen.  Second
is that the more specific function may not be visible to the compiler (hidden behind an API).  Note
that the first failure case should not actually apply here.  When we statically know that we have
a ${\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$, we actually know much more than this.  The self-type idiom means
that this type is equivalent to $\mathbb{Z}$.  But $\mathbb{Z} <: \mathbb{Q} <: {\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Q}}$
which implies that based on static information {\it def2} should apply.  However, this does not extend to
the second failure case when the more specific definition is hidden.

One way to ensure that the first situation cannot happen is to rewrite the overload so that the self-type
is a bound rather than the parameter type:\\

$\begin{array}{l}
{\it add}\ob{X <:{\tt Ring}\ob{X}}(X,X) : X~(*){\it def1}\\
{\it add}\ob{Y <: {\tt Field}\ob{Y}}(Y,Y) : Y~(*){\it def2}\\
\end{array}$\\

This forces us to recognize the type ${\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$ as $\mathbb{Z}$ in order for {\it def1} to
apply which will automatically also mean that {\it def2} applies.  This approach suggests further that
the self-type idiom should be more than simply an idiom and instead a separate construct which cannot
be used as a first class type, but instead only in bounds.  Victor and John have started working on this
sort of theory with their {\it trolls}.  However, the visibility problem shows that this is not sufficient to fix the
unsoundness problems with the cross instantiation.  Therefore, more work needs to be done in order
to understand how to best support the numerical hierarchy in the Fortress type system.

%\section{Fortress Features, Design, and Related Work}
%

A trait or object declaration may have \emph{static parameters}, 
in which case it defines a \emph{generic type} with those parameters.
% Victor: We might prefer to define generic type in its own section, 
%   so that it applies to all types, not just trait types.
%   I'm not sure we ever need to talk about other generic types though:
%   all the types in extends/excludes/comprises clauses must be trait types.
A generic type is \emph{not} a (first-order) type; 
% (i.e., it does not represent a set of values);
rather,
it is a \emph{type schema} 
whose parameters must be \emph{instantiated} 
with \emph{static arguments} 
to produce a trait type.
The resulting type is an \emph{instantiation} 
% (with the arguments) 
of the generic type.
% Victor: Does this sentence belong here?  (Perhaps only in traits chapter.)
The trait or object declaration may impose conditions on the arguments 
with which its static parameters may be instantiated.
% Victor: I had "with which the generic type may be instantiated"
%   which does not technically follow the terminology established above,
%   though I don't think anyone would be confused.
See \chapref{traits} for more of static parameters 
and how they may be instantiated.

For convenience, 
we consider a trait or object declaration without static parameters
to define a generic type (with no parameters)
whose unique instantiation 
is the trait type defined by the declaration.
Thus, 
properties of instantiations of generic types 
also apply to trait types defined by 
non-parameterized trait and object declarations.

% Victor: I just made up this terminology.
...
Fortress also imposes a rule called \emph{instantiation exclusion}:
% which defines the exclusion relation for different instantiations of a generic type:
Two instantiations of a generic trait type exclude each other 
if the corresponding arguments for any covariant parameter exclude each other, 
or if the corresponding arguments for any non-covariant parameter 
are not type equivalent.
\note{I believe this exactly characterizes exclusion
among different instantiations of a generic type, 
but the rule we impose is stronger:
Any trait that extends (possibly indirectly) 
two instantiations of a generic type 
must extend an \emph{expressible} instantiation of that generic type 
that is a subtype of both.
In other words,
among all instantiations of a generic type 
that are supertypes of some expressible trait type, 
one must be a subtype of all the others, 
and it must be expressible.
This section should say only which instantiations exclude each other,
as it does.
It perhaps should make it clearer that what is said here 
is a consequence of instantiation exclusion, 
which is a rule applied to trait declarations.}


% An object trait type is a leaf type:
An object trait type has no strict subtype other than \Bottom, 
and it excludes any type that is not its supertype.

A trait declaration may have a \KWD{comprises} clause, 
which also specifies a set of types and 
generic types determined by the generic type of the declaration.
An instantiation of the generic type defined by such a declaration 
is covered by the union 
of the types in this set 
and the corresponding instantiations of the generic type in this set.

% Victor: I'm not sure about the proper terminology here.
A trait or object declaration may provide a \emph{coercion} from a type or a generic type.
(See \secref{coercion-decl} and \chapref{coercion}.)
If a trait or object declaration provides a coercion from a type, 
then any instantiation of the generic type defined by that declaration 
coerces that type.
If it provides a coercion from a generic type, 
then an instantiation of the generic type defined by that declaration

\subsection{The type of \KWD{self} in a trait with a self-type parameter}
\seclabel{revival-self-type}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{idn-ref}; \secref{trait-decls}; \secref{methods}.
\item[Change] In \secref{idn-ref}, a sentence after the one on the self-type
idiom: in a declaration of a trait \VAR{T} with no \KWD{comprises} clause, or one that lists only ``\EXP{\ldots}'', and a
self-type parameter \VAR{X}, \KWD{self} has the type \EXP{T \cap X} in the bodies of
the trait's methods, and the \KWD{self} parameter keeps the type \VAR{T} in the
signature of each method declaration.
In \secref{trait-decls}, a paragraph after the one on \KWD{comprises} clauses
defines a self-type parameter: a static parameter of a trait with no
\KWD{comprises} clause, or one that lists only ``\EXP{\ldots}'', that is bounded by the trait at its own static
parameters, or by an instantiation of a trait with a self-type parameter that the
trait also lists in its \KWD{extends} clause, with that static parameter as the
static argument for the self-type parameter.
The paragraph requires every trait or object declaration and every object
expression that extends an instantiation of such a trait to be a subtype of
the static argument of that instantiation for the self-type parameter, a trait
standing as the type of \KWD{self} in its bodies, the intersection of its type with the types
its \KWD{comprises} clause lists or with its own self-type parameter, and gives an example marked ``Not allowed''.
In \secref{methods}, a box after the sentence that a functional method's
\KWD{self} parameter implicitly has the type of the enclosing trait or object
says that the sentence still holds of the declaration's signature.
Each of the three passages has a box.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; it follows the
revival's decision of 13~October 2026 on the bodies of the self-typed traits,
and its second form of a self-type parameter, through a trait that the trait
extends, follows a default taken under that decision on 14~October 2026.
\library\ declare their orders and their algebra as traits whose static
parameter is bounded by the trait itself, as in
\EXP{\KWD{trait}\;\TYP{Integral}\llbracket{}I \KWD{extends} \TYP{Integral}\llbracket{}I\rrbracket\rrbracket},
and give them default bodies that return \KWD{self} where that parameter is
declared, or pass it where the parameter is expected: the team's minimal
complete definitions, such as \OPR{MIN} on \TYP{StandardTotalOrder} and
\VAR{floor} on \TYP{Integral}.
The interpreter runs them; the compiled type checker refused 29 of them,
since it typed \KWD{self} as the trait.
A bound constrains the static argument, not \KWD{self}: an object may extend
\EXP{\TYP{Integral}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}32\rrbracket} without being a
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and a body that treats \KWD{self} as the parameter is sound
only if every declaration that extends the trait is a subtype of its static
argument for that parameter.
Scala states that rule for its declared self types (``The self type of a class
or object must conform to the self types of all classes which are inherited by
the template'', \emph{Scala Language Specification 2.13}, section 5.1); the revival reads the self type from the bound, which \library\
already write, as the team's compiled type checker reads it from a
\KWD{comprises} clause (\secref{idn-ref}), a reading that the team's gated test
\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXX10k.test} pins.
Naden's account of the Return Type Rule (2012) asked that the self-type idiom
become ``a separate construct which cannot be used as a first class type, but
instead only in bounds''
(\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex}, lines 626--630).
The signatures keep the type of the trait because the type group's account of
overloading of 2019 (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, POPL 2019) assumes, for the
completeness of its matching of types, that no declared type holds a type
parameter inside an intersection (pp.~11:21--22), and its Return Type Rule
compares declared domains (p.~11:13): with the intersection in the signatures,
the domains of the two declarations of \OPR{CMP} on \TYP{StandardPartialOrder}
and \TYP{StandardTotalOrder} became equivalent, and the compiled type checker
reported 18 errors of the Return Type Rule that the declarations do not make.
The second form of a self-type parameter keeps valid as written the mixins of
\library\ that the team wrote in 2009, \TYP{ContainmentBySubset} and
\TYP{ContainmentByComparison}, whose static parameter is bounded by the trait
\TYP{Containment}, which they extend at it.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/self-typed-bodies-judgement.md} and
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-self-type/decision-record.md} in the
revival's repository.
\item[Effect] The compiled type checker types \KWD{self} as \EXP{T \cap X} in
the bodies of the dotted and functional methods of a trait with a self
parameter \VAR{X}, keeps \VAR{T} in the signatures that overloading, the Return
Type Rule and the choice of a declaration at a call read, and refuses a trait
or object declaration or an object expression that the new paragraph of
\secref{trait-decls} does not allow, with the message
``\VAR{D} extends \EXP{C\llbracket{}A\rrbracket}, whose self parameter is \VAR{A},
but \VAR{D} is not a subtype of \VAR{A}.''.
The interpreter has no static types: it runs the bodies as before, and loads a
declaration that the paragraph refuses.
The code generator compiles a default body that returns \KWD{self} as the self
parameter with no conversion to the type of the instance, so a program that
runs such a body, which the compiled type checker now accepts, with the parameter at an object type
fails the JVM's verification when the body's class is loaded (row~695 of the revival's gap
ledger).
\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/var-ref.tex},
lines 53--54 and 64--69, which stand unchanged and are now followed by the new
sentence:
\begin{quote}
The type of \KWD{self} is the type of the trait or object being declared by
the innermost enclosing trait or object declaration or object expression.
\end{quote}
and
\begin{quote}
If the innermost enclosing such construct is a trait declaration (for a trait
called, say, `\EXP{T}'), and that trait declaration has a \KWD{comprises}
clause, and `\EXP{U_1}', `\EXP{U_2}', ..., `\EXP{U_n}' are the traits mentioned
in the \KWD{comprises} clause, then the type of \KWD{self} is instead
``\EXP{T \cap (U_{\mathrm{1}} \cup U_{\mathrm{2}} \cup \ldots \cup U_{\mathrm{n}})}''.
\end{quote}
The paragraph of \secref{trait-decls} is new.
\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/traits.tex}, line 486, the end of the
sentence of \secref{methods} that the new box follows, stands unchanged:
\begin{quote}
and implicitly has the type of the enclosing trait or object.
\end{quote}
\item[Route C] Under route~C a self-typed trait is read by a \KWD{comprises}
clause that lists its static parameter, as the compiled path's own library
declares its orders (\nolinkurl{Library/CompilerAlgebra.fsi}, lines 16 and 24,
in the revival's repository); under such a clause the self-type idiom of
\secref{idn-ref} types \KWD{self}, and this rule is not reached.
A return to that form would need the clause on the self-typed traits of
\library, which would also close each of them to its static parameter; a way
for the interpreter past its stack overflow on a clause that lists a static
parameter (row~407 of the revival's gap ledger); and leave in
\secref{trait-decls} for a static parameter as a listed type, which the type
group's calculus of 2012 does not admit.
\end{description}

\subsection{Passages not yet revised}
\seclabel{revival-notrevised}

No passage that instantiation exclusion or the reorganized numeric types
contradict is known to be unrevised.
The rule by which a generic call over two different integer types
infers the narrowest type that both coerce into is written into
\chapref{type-inference} together with its implementation
(\secref{revival-inference}); the passages that chapter left unrevised, the
sentences of \chapref{multiple-dispatch} by which static parameters were
inferred before the applicability of a declaration was checked and before
declarations were compared, the implicit bound of \secref{type-param}, and the
rule of \chapref{overloaded-declarations} on a naked type parameter of bound
\TYP{Any}, are revised with the overloading chapters (\secref{revival-overloading},
\secref{revival-bound}).
The instance of a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter of a declaration that a call
reaches only by dispatch, where nothing fixes it at run time, is not described;
the rule of \secref{resolving-overloading} is for type parameters (row~446 of the
revival's gap ledger).
The sentence of \secref{where-clauses} that a \KWD{where}-clause variable may
not appear as a static argument in an \KWD{extends} clause also refuses a
variable that a constraint fixes to one type; whether it is to be narrowed is
not settled.
The Meet Rule for dotted methods (\secref{more-specific-rule}) asks for a
declaration on the intersection of two parameter types; whether declarations
that together cover the intersection satisfy it too is not settled.
The type of a static call whose argument's static type stands between two
traits with \KWD{comprises} clauses, where its most specific declarations, or a
declaration more specific than them that the call may run, have static
parameters, is not given (\secref{revival-meet}).
Whether two parameter types exclude each other when the only static arguments
at which they could meet are ones that a bound rules out is not settled: the
compiled type checker takes them to exclude where the static argument that the
two parameter types force is a named type that fails the bound, and not where
it would reason through the ancestors of the parameter types
(\secref{overloading-static-params}).
Whether a \KWD{nat} parameter, which may appear wherever a variable of type
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} can (\secref{natparams}), may be a component of a range is
settled (\secref{revival-inference}): it converts to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} as an
integer numeral does, so the static ranges of \secref{ranges} and the examples
whose ranges a \KWD{nat} parameter bounds stand as written.
Before the number chapters were revised, this section said:
\begin{quote}
The number chapters, \chapref{lib:numbers-basic} (whose integers are \secref{basic-integers})
and \chapref{lib:numbers-advanced}, are not yet revised.
Their nested tower, in which each integer type is a subtype of the rational
one above it and each carries its algebra at its own type, and the
conditional self-extension of \TYP{RationalQuantity}, are refused by
instantiation exclusion, as the compiled type checker refuses the
library's nested tower today.
They will be revised together with the reorganization of the library's
numeric types that route~A decides, and not before, because a
specification ahead of its library is as much an open discrepancy as one
behind it.
Until then the rule refuses the tower these chapters describe.
\end{quote}

<!-- The Fable judgement on PLAN item 58, answering the curator's question of 2026-10-19: whether a combination of declarations can rebuild, in the flat number tower, what the Working Draft's tower gave an integer raised to a negative power, case by case (an unsigned exponent, a signed computed one, a numeral, a float or rational base); every way the language and the library offer, with its cases, cost and evidence; the least bad mix; and what each way reverses or reads anew among his decisions. Written on `main` at `3f463d3b5`; it measures one thing (section 8) and cites the rest. -->

# The Fable judgement on item 58: can a combination rebuild the tower's power?

**Answer in five lines.** No, not whole. An unsigned exponent and a float or rational base are rebuilt already, by the declarations the library has. A signed computed exponent can be rebuilt by type, as contract R, at R's cost; it rebuilds the Working Draft's rule, which the team's own code and tests never followed, so the premise he took excludes it. A numeral exponent cannot be rebuilt: a numeral's sign never reaches a type on either path, and under walk a numeral has no type of its own until Q-walk, so no overload can split `10^16` from `10^(-16)`. That is the only case the team's tests reach at a negative exponent, so the hole is where the tests are.

**Recommendation and default.** E, as PLAN item 58's default: the integer's own type at every exponent, `IntegerOverflow` where the result is not an integer, `DivisionByZero` at a base of 0, ±1 exact; a float or rational base for a fraction, as the library already does; `fail[\ZZ32\]` in `strToInt`; the three team tests and the two demos written with a float base. It is itself the combination he is looking for, split on the other operand: the base's type says whether a negative exponent has a value, and the sign of the exponent, a value, is tested at run time, as the library tests every such subset (P-80). He can take it without reading on. Nothing in it reverses a decision on record.

Short names: REPORT is `explorations/perf-probes/integer-power/REPORT.md`; the review is `explorations/reviews/integer-power-negative-exponent.md`; the digest is `explorations/reviews/digest-2026-10-19.md`; B.2 is section B.2 of `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-10-19-haiku/fable-judgement.md`; `P-` is a POSITIONS entry, `F-` a FACTS entry, "row" a gap-ledger row; a bare `fss:N` is `Library/FortressLibrary.fss` and `fsi:N` its api; `Builtin.fss:N` is `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss`; the Working Draft is `Specification-1.0-frozen/`.

## 0. Words, for a reader who knows Swift and the JVM

- `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` are `Int32` and `Int64`; `NN32`, `NN64` are `UInt32` and `UInt64`; `ZZ` is a `BigInteger`; `QQ` is an exact fraction of two `ZZ`; `RR64` is a `Double`; `IntLiteral` is the type of a numeral such as `16` before it converts into one of them (F-79; `Builtin.fss:484`).
- **Flat.** None of these is a subtype of another, as Swift's integer types are not. Each wider type declares a `coerce` from each narrower one, and the conversion is applied for you, but only when no declaration fits the argument as it is (P-74; F-131; `Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:474-478`). `Number` is above them all and has no operators of its own (P-43; `fss:380-396`).
- **The tower** is the Working Draft's design, where ℕ ⊂ ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ were subtypes (section 2).
- **Overloading** chooses, among the declarations of one name, the most specific that applies to the arguments. Fortress does this at run time by the arguments' run-time types, as Julia does, besides the checker's static choice (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex:298-310`; the `fortress-repo` skill, "Dispatch is on every argument, at run time"). A declaration is chosen by types, never by values.
- **A numeral** has one type on the compiled path, `IntLiteral`, whatever its value (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Misc.scala:468-469`). Under walk it is an `Int`, a `ZZ32` value (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java:1635-1637`; `.../evaluator/values/FIntLiteral.java:40-50`; F-74). **Q-walk** is the step that gives walk's numeral the type `IntLiteral`; it waits for the switch-over and is not designed (P-76; `explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md:86`; digest, section 5, item 3).
- **The distance** is the count of the compiled checker's errors over the interpreter's library, 34 today, six of them at integer powers (digest, sections 1 and 2; F-241). **The quick pair** is microGPT's walk check, two programs, 7 checks each (the review, "Words used here").
- **E, Z, R, X** are the four contracts of the ask: an error, zero, a rational typed by the exponent, an exponent typed so that it cannot be negative (REPORT, section 3).

## 1. His question, and the three facts the coordinator gave him

His words, as the coordinator cleaned them (the brief holds the raw text):

> I need more context to make an informed decision. This seems like a consequence of flattening the numeric tower, and much of the existing library design depends on this tower. None of the options seem to fit, because it's not a one-size-fits-all kind of solution that can cover all cases. I feel we likely need a combination of several options to rebuild the original behavior of the numeric tower, but at the same time I worry that might not be possible in the current design. I would like Fable to weigh in on this. Can't we somehow use clever overloads to split the negative exponents away from the positive ones? But I guess there's no way to attempt a coercion to NN when the exponents are already ZZ… Before asking Fable: do you see where I am going with this? Is that an unreasonable direction?

The direction is reasonable, and it is the right instinct: split by type. The answer below says which types can carry the split in the flat design (the base's type, and for the exponent only an unsigned width) and which cannot (the sign of a `ZZ32`, and the sign of a numeral). The three facts the coordinator told him are checked:

1. **Overloading picks by the arguments' types, never by their values, on both paths.** Confirmed. The specification dispatches "the declarations that are applicable to that call at run time" by the arguments' dynamic types (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex:298-310`); walk dispatches on run-time classes (`.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/interpreter.md`, "How walk evaluates a program"); the checker on static types. The one place the Working Draft put a value into a type was the numeral: `NaturalNumeral[\n,10,v\]`, with the value `v` a static parameter (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-85`). The revival's `IntLiteral` carries none (P-76; `Misc.scala:468-469`).
2. **Nothing converts a `ZZ32` into an `NN32` implicitly.** Confirmed, and stronger than stated. `NN32` declares one coercion, from `IntLiteral` (`Builtin.fss:386`); `NN64` from `NN32` and `IntLiteral` (`fss:911-912`). The explicit conversion, `unsigned(self): NN32` on `ZZ32` (`fss:806`), reinterprets the bits: `unsigned(-1)` is `4294967295`, measured (section 8). And since a coercion is chosen by type, like an overload (`conversions-coercions.tex:474-478`), a declared `ZZ32` to `NN32` coercion could not refuse a negative value either: it would convert it as `unsigned` does. So "attempt a coercion to NN" cannot be a sign test, as he guessed.
3. **R is already a split by type.** Confirmed: an unsigned or numeral exponent gives the base's type and a signed one gives `QQ`, six declarations per integer type (REPORT, section 3.2).

One more point on his premise, "much of the existing library design depends on this tower". It does, in one sense and not in another. The library as the team wrote it rested on the integers being floats: in 2008, `trait Integral extends { StandardTotalOrder[\Integral\], RR64 }`, so the declared `RR64` of every integer power held both the integer of a nonnegative power and the float of a negative one (REPORT, section 6; row 438). It never rested on ℤ ⊂ ℚ for the power: no native ever produced a rational (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/Int.java:222-231`). The flat tower removed the first (d846e3644, 2026-09-27), and the six sites are the residue (F-241). So the question is which leg of the tower, if any, to put back, and section 2 names the legs.

## 2. What the tower gave, and what it rested on

### 2.1 The Working Draft, case by case

- **An unsigned exponent.** ℕ was a synonym for ℤ≥, the nonnegative integers (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:65`), itself a subtype of ℤ and of ℚ≥ (`:37-38`). ℤ declared `opr ^(self, power: ℕ): ℤ`, "Exponentiation of an integer to a nonnegative integer power produces an integer result" (`:137`; `git show 5a68404fd:Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex`, lines 506-510). The result: an integer.
- **A signed computed exponent.** ℤ's power does not apply to a ℤ exponent. But ℤ extended ℚ (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:195-196`), and ℚ declared `opr ^(self, power: ℤ): ℚ#`, "Exponentiation of a rational number to an integer power produces a rational result", with `x^y = 1/(x^(-y))` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/numbers.tex:344-355`). So `2^n` with `n: ℤ` was a rational, by type, also when `n` held 3. To get an integer back, a program wrote a run-time check: `check≥(self): ℤ≥ throws CastError` (`basic-integers.tex:181-192`, the twelve check methods).
- **A numeral.** A numeral is digits and letters, with no sign (`Specification/basic/lexical-structure.tex:1053-1080`). A digits-only numeral had the type `NaturalNumeral[\n,10,v\]` (`literals.tex:83-85`), so `2^3` chose ℤ's power and stayed an integer. `-16` is the prefix operator `-` applied to the numeral `16`, a ℤ, so `10^(-16)` chose ℚ's power and gave the rational 1/10^16; and `7.07 10^(-1)` was ℝ times ℚ, fine because ℚ ⊂ ℝ (`numbers.tex:36-37`).
- **A float or rational base.** ℝ's and ℚ's own powers, at any integer exponent.

### 2.2 The three legs, and where each went

The tower's answer rested on three things, and the revival set each aside by a decision of his:

- **L1, subtyping among the number types**, ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ, so that a ℤ exponent reached ℚ's method and a ℚ result flowed into ℝ code. Gone with the flat tower, by the exclusion rule (P-43).
- **L2, a numeral type that carries its value**, hence its sign. Set aside for the compiler library's `IntLiteral` (P-76, "taken over the specification's unfinished numeral types").
- **L3, sign-refined types with run-time checks**, ℤ≥ and `check≥`; in the later chapter, the refinements are boolean static parameters of one trait, which the exclusion rule refuses, and "the way back is the later chapter's declaration-site variance: each flag a covariant static parameter" (`Specification/advanced-lib/numbers-advanced.tex:14-31`, `:34-45`). Superseded (P-80: "a program tests such a subset at run time"); their return waits on covariance (P-62; row 404).

### 2.3 The team's later word: the code

The code never ran the Working Draft's rule. The interpreter's library typed every integer power `RR64`, on a tower where every integer was an `RR64`, with natives that answer the integer for a nonnegative exponent and a float for a negative one (REPORT, section 6; `Int.java:222-231`). The compiled prelude typed `ZZ32 ^ ZZ32 : ZZ32`, `NN32 ^ NN32 : NN32` and `NN64 ^ NN64 : NN64` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:267`, `:326`, `:385`; `.fss:744`): the exponent's type is the base's, signed where the base is, and the result is the base's type at every exponent; its negative case is the cast of `Math.pow`, 0 (row 523; row 441). Steele's `intToIntPower` is bound nowhere (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleIntArith.java:380-398`). And the team's own tests use a signed computed exponent as an integer: `p = 2^(k-1)` then `p BITOR (p-1)` (`ProjectFortress/library_tests/ShiftTest2.fss:19-20`), `d = 2^n'` compared with a `ZZ32` (`ProjectFortress/tests/zeno.fss:57`), and the library's `strToInt`, `d radix^(n-i)` summed in a `SUM[\ZZ32\]` (`fss:4540-4541`). Under the Working Draft's rule each of these is a rational.

So the later word, which outweighs the earlier text (P-26), is: an integer `^` gives the integer's own type at a signed exponent. That is the premise he took (PLAN item 58; B.2, first point). On the value at a negative exponent the code is silent, as B.2 found: a cast's by-product and an unbound helper are not a position.

## 3. The answer, case by case

| case | the tower gave | the flat design can give | by which way | at what cost |

The probe worker returned this text when the harness refused it a report file; the coordinating session wrote it here unchanged on 2026-10-16. The worktree `/home/user/fortress-probe-where` holds the patches and the new tests.

# `where` clauses and the distance to the switch-over: a measurement

This is a measurement probe on the branch `wip/probe-where-clauses`, in the worktree `/home/user/fortress-probe-where`. The worktree was seeded from the base build `/home/user/fortress-base16` (`528438ac5`; `main` at `d731fc328` has changed no code since). The edits are uncommitted in the worktree; the patches are quoted inline below. There are two parts, written in this order and kept apart:

- **Part A** is the brief: library edits that use no new language, and what the code generator does with `NatParam`'s clause. Part A was finished and written before Part B began.
- **Part B** is the curator's addition, sent mid-task: the narrow `where`-clause forms, built as shadow patches in the compiled checker.

---

# Part A: library edits with no new language

## A.0 In short

| Group (ledger row) | Errors | Cause | Library edit that clears it |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SUM`'s fusion pairs with `MAX` and `MIN` (433) | 6 | Four errors: `SumReduction` (bound `AdditiveGroup`) names `MaxReduction[\T\]`, `MinReduction[\T\]` and their pairs, whose bounds it does not meet. Two errors: the `distribute` overloads answer a pair over `Maybe[\T\]`, where the inherited `distribute` answers a pair over `T`. No bound fixes those two. | **Yes: removal.** Only the team's experimental `Generator2` reaches these declarations, and none of its answers change. A `where` clause would clear only 4 of the 6. |
| `AnyList`'s `\|\|`, `addLeft`, `addRight`, and the list comprehension's unwrap (636) | 4 | `AnyList` and `AnyCovColl` are supertraits with no element type. Their bodies call functions that need a `List[\E\]` or a `CovariantCollection[\T\]`. | **Yes.** `\|\|` moves into `List[\E\]` through one private generic helper. `addLeft`/`addRight` become `singleton(e) \|\| self`. The unwrap takes `cast[\CovariantCollection[\T\]\]`. Walk prints the same 14 lines on a probe before and after. |

# Q1 of climb batch 16: the detour toward Scala's way

## In short

- **The question.** May the compiled checker refuse `object O extends { A, B }`, where `A` declares `pick(self)` abstract and `B` gives it a body, and `O` declares none of its own (rows 572 and 727)?
- **The answer.** Refuse it (P-149), the curator's word of 06:23 UTC: the specification's text and the type group's later calculus refuse it, and the revival does not bend Fortress toward another language for a convenience.
- **The detour.** The ask put to the curator led him toward Scala's way, which accepts `O`. He pre-recorded it, then learnt that the specification refuses `O`, and took the refusal.
- **Its cost.** About 1.7M tokens written: the probe 0.56M, and this session 1.17M, nearly all of it two rewrites of its 550K context into the cache after the VM restart and after a gap of nearly two hours.
- **The causes.** The ask did not say first what the designers' text says and which way it points. It named a peer language's behaviour as if it were an option of equal standing. It used the record's shorthand. And the fact that would decide the question, whether the library uses the shape, was not measured before the ask.

## The question

A functional method has `self` among its parameters and is called like a function, `pick(x)`. A trait may leave one abstract, with no body:

```
trait A  pick(self): String  end           (* abstract *)
trait B  pick(self): String = "b"  end     (* a body *)
object O extends { A, B } end              (* no pick of its own *)
```

Today the compiled path accepts `O` and runs `B`'s body, because its overloading check skips a component's own abstract functional methods (`OverloadingChecker.scala:139-141`). Walk refuses `O` at load (F-142). Separately, an abstract and a concrete declaration of one method in one trait pass the checker and crash the code generator (row 727).

## How it went, in UTC

- **01:08 to 01:37.** Batch 16's planner drafted Q1 with the default "refuse" (rung K builds it), and listed the sources: the specification, the type group's rules, the team's dotted-method check and Java refuse; the team's abstract-method check and Scala accept. Its brief told it to run no new probe, so the record left the library's use of the shape to rung K's own run.
- **01:38 to 02:11.** The Fable review agreed that Q1 is the curator's.
- **02:13.** The coordinator put Q1 to the curator. The ask used the record's words ("batch 8's judge", "item 62", "read them", "leave them unread"), gave the sources as a split without saying that the specification's text refuses `O`, and gave as the refusal's cost that it "gives up Scala's way of letting a sibling trait supply the body".
- **04:18.** The curator found the ask unreadable past its primer, leaned to Scala's way if it had a clean resolution, and asked why the library's use of the shape had not been measured, "the most important factor for the decision".

\newsec{\Any, \Bottom\ and the Type Hierarchy}{type-hierarchy}
\seclabel{bottom-type}

Types are partially ordered by subtyping (see \secref{subtyping}),
which defines the \emph{type hierarchy}.
\Any\ is the top of the type hierarchy:
every type is a subtype of \Any\
and every value belongs to \Any.
% and every value is an instance of \Any.
The only type that \Any\ excludes is \Bottom.

\Bottom\ is the bottom of the type hierarchy:
every type is a supertype of \Bottom.
It is \emph{uninhabited}: 
% Do we want to define this term?  
% I don't know that we use it anywhere.
no value belongs to \Bottom,  
%no value is an instance of \Bottom
and \Bottom\ excludes every type (including itself).
\Bottom\ is the only type that excludes itself.
\Bottom\ is also inexpressible:
it cannot be written in a program 
(see \secref{expressible-types})

\redundant[\secref{subtyping}]

\note{Victor: 
Commented out definition of \emph{leaf type}.}
\newsec{Tuple Types}{tuple-types}

\begin{Grammar}
\emph{TupleType} &::=&
\texttt{(} \emph{Type}\EXP{,} \emph{TypeList} \texttt{)}\\

\emph{TypeList} &::=& \emph{Type}(\EXP{,} \emph{Type})$^*$
\end{Grammar}

A tuple type consists of a parenthesized, comma-separated list
of two or more types.

Every tuple type is a supertype of \Bottom, 
and a subtype of \Any.
No other type is a supertype of all tuple types.
Tuple types are \emph{covariant}:
a tuple type $X$ is a subtype of tuple type $Y$
if and only if they have the same number of element types
and each element type of $X$ 
is a subtype of the corresponding element type of $Y$.

A tuple type excludes \Bottom, \Void, and every trait type, arrow type or function type.
A tuple type excludes every tuple type 
that does not have the same number of element types.
Also, tuple types with the same number of element types exclude each other
if any pair of corresponding element types exclude each other.

Tuple types $X$ and $Y$ that do not exclude each other 
must have the same number of elements, 
and their intersection is defined elementwise:
the intersection of $X$ and $Y$ 
is equivalent to a tuple type with the same number of elements 
in which each element type 
is the intersection of the corresponding element types of $X$ and $Y$.
(The intersection of tuple types---or any types---that exclude each other 
is \Bottom.)


In addition, every trait type is a subtype of \TYP{Any}.

A trait declaration may also include an \KWD{excludes} clause,
in which case the defined trait type
excludes every type that appears in that clause.
Every trait type also excludes every arrow type and every tuple type,
and the special types \TYP{()} and \TYP{BottomType}.

\subsection{Object Trait Types}
A tuple type consists of a parenthesized, comma-separated list
of two or more types.

Every tuple type is a subtype of \TYP{Any}.
No other type encompasses all tuple types.
Tuple types cannot be extended by trait types.
Tuple types are covariant:
a tuple type $X$ is a subtype of tuple type $Y$
if and only if they have the same number of element types
and each element type of $X$ is a subtype of the
corresponding element type of $Y$.

A tuple type excludes any non-tuple type
other than \TYP{Any}.
A tuple type excludes every tuple type that does not have the same
number of element types.
Also, tuple types that have the same number of element types exclude each other
if any pair of corresponding element types exclude each other.
